column1: Mimicking

If you were God, how would the world be different? If I were God, there would be neither atheists nor believers because there would be no need for belief. All would know, as I know, the essential truths that bind us together. The concept of faith, as it is now understood, would be rendered obsolete. There would be no fear of death because there would be no death: only a perpetual state of evolving awareness. There would be no wars, no famines, no disease, no injustice, no poverty: only an endless exploration of existence. Because "evil," as we conceive it, would be an impossibility, there would be no such thing as forgiveness, since there would be nothing to forgive. The word "sin" would not exist in any language, and any concept remotely like it would be utterly meaningless. Love would be the only law, since love would be the only truth. And every creature, from the smallest microbe to the largest galaxy, would be imbued with a profound sense of wonder and gratitude for the gift of existence.

Did Moses go to Heaven in the Bible? If not, why didn't he go to Heaven? Moses did not go to Heaven, according to the Bible, and this is made quite clear in Deuteronomy 34, where God shows Moses the Promised Land, but then says he will not be allowed to enter it. The reason given is that Moses, at least on one occasion, disobeyed God’s command and failed to honor Him as holy when striking a rock for water, rather than speaking to it, despite the fact that the Israelites were dying of thirst. This act of disobedience, whether great or small, prevented Moses from attaining the ultimate reward. His body was buried in an undisclosed location "in a valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor," and that was that. No ascension, no heavenly choir, no pearly gates. He simply was not allowed to go to God’s home. In the New Testament, Jesus Christ is presented as the one bridge between humanity and the divine realm. Moses was a great leader, a prophet, a lawgiver, but not divine, and was also a man subject to mortality, weakness, and sin. Jesus, according to the Gospels, conquered death and ascended to Heaven, opening the doors for those who believe in Him. For Moses, the Promised Land was the horizon; for believers in Christ, Heaven is promised.

If Jesus took human flesh, how can he be sinless? IF HUMAN, THEN NOT SINLESS? by Michael R. Burch  The question presupposes the answer, and isn’t meant to be a question at all. It’s a challenge. It contains a premise that is both specious and dubious. The premise? That humans are, by nature, sinful. Is this really the case? What exactly constitutes a "sin"? The ancient Greeks, for example, might have considered it a “sin” to avoid beauty, art and intellect. The ancient Hindus might consider it sinful to forsake one's dharma. If the premise is that the ancient Greeks and Hindus also are all sinners, then the claim of Jesus also being human, but sinless still seems to be problematic. What, then, did Jesus do? Or did not do? Did he fail to live up to the highest standards that had yet been set? Did he forsake his dharma? We are told he did not. Then there is the “problem” of the divine component: if he were wholly divine, he would have been incapable of sin, perhaps not “human” at all. But if divine, then not human. And so the paradox. And so the conundrum. So there he lies, a riddle. And this, after two millennia, still gives the faithful pause. Or should. The question is answered in faith and in the heart. Not in logic. The mind is unable to unravel this. This is the ultimate in faith. Or the ultimate, in faith. The heart does not, cannot doubt. And will not. It is beyond us, or “above” us. And we shall never know. We can only feel, and believe. We can only love, and have faith. Or not.

I see many people online arguing for Jesus mythicism. However, I have also read in several places that scholars reconsider this a fringe theory. Do many mainstream scholars doubt the existence of an itinerant preacher named Jesus of Nazareth? Yes, the vast majority of mainstream scholars, including historians, theologians, and biblical scholars, accept the historical existence of Jesus of Nazareth. This consensus is based on various lines of evidence, including the New Testament texts, which, despite their theological nature, contain historical details consistent with the time and place in which Jesus is said to have lived. Additionally, non-Christian sources like the writings of the Roman historians Tacitus and Pliny the Younger also offer evidence of Jesus’s existence, though these references are often brief and indirect. While there are varying interpretations of specific events and the nature of Jesus's divinity, the general consensus among scholars is that an itinerant preacher named Jesus did, in fact, live and have a following in first-century Palestine. The arguments for Jesus mythicism, which claim that Jesus was a mythological figure and not a historical person, are usually rejected as lacking substantial evidence. These claims are considered fringe theories because they often rely on selective readings of ancient texts and a dismissal of the established historical and archaeological context.

How did Jesus turn water into wine at the wedding in Cana? Some apologists have tried to explain away this miracle of Jesus, suggesting that the water somehow possessed the elements of wine already. However, this explanation seems implausible: the water was clearly in one state, wine in another. And if Jesus's powers were limited, why would he choose the conversion of ordinary water into a fine, vintage wine, which suggests an abundance of creative power? The obvious explanation is that we should not attempt to diminish a miracle, but should simply note that Jesus had the power to do astonishing, wonderful things, from the very beginning.

Who are some notable poets in Russia today? The question has no easy answer, as Russia, despite—or perhaps because of—its turbulent history, boasts a thriving literary scene, though it is often more underground than in Western nations. Much like the avant-garde movements of the early 20th century, some of the most compelling poets today are those outside the mainstream, writing in defiance of a state that often seeks to control artistic expression. One cannot speak of contemporary Russian poetry, or any art form, without acknowledging the pervasive influence of the political climate. Censorship and restrictions on freedom of speech, particularly since the annexation of Crimea, have created a challenging environment for artists who dare to speak truth to power. Some poets have chosen exile, while others navigate this landscape with skill and subtlety, writing with an elegance that both critiques and endures. Among the most acclaimed are those, who, like Anna Akhmatova or Osip Mandelstam before them, capture the spirit of their time with words. Some focus on the everyday lives of ordinary people, while others delve into complex philosophical and historical themes. Many young poets experiment with new forms and styles, incorporating elements of rap, spoken word, and digital media. It’s a dynamic and complex world, full of innovation and struggle, where the power of poetry remains a potent force.

What is a poem on the moon in any specific language? I have long been fascinated by the moon, especially when it casts its spell on the world in a language I can barely understand. Take, for instance, the Japanese word for the moon, "tsuki," which sounds so ethereal and delicate, like a whispered secret. I found a few poems about the moon, written in Japanese, that I’ve tried to decipher with varying degrees of success. One poem speaks of the moon’s reflection on a lake - shimmering "tsuki no kagami" - and in the shimmering, the poet seems to find a piece of heaven. Another poem, more melancholic perhaps, speaks of the moon's cold beauty reflected in the tears of a woman. The best one I’ve found, though, speaks of the moon in the language of the heart. It has these lines, which I take to mean something like, “The moon is a beacon in the darkness, a guide through the storms of life.” Perhaps the moon, like poetry, speaks to us most clearly when expressed in the language of the soul.

How could Adam and Eve be white when the first humans lived in Africa? If you doubt the Bible, I can offer a little-known insight: neither Adam nor Eve has even a passing resemblance to the individuals portrayed in the illustrated versions of the Book of Genesis. Adam, by the Hebrew meaning, simply means "human." Eve means "life." And the Garden of Eden may be nothing more than a metaphor, a parable, a poetic myth, or some amalgamation of the three. I would not waste considerable time on this question, unless you have nothing better to do with the countless hours available in life. And it is always interesting to question all that we’ve been told, all we’d like to believe, and all we’d prefer to think. Questioning is a good habit, even if the questions have no definitive answers.

What was Helen of Troy's fate after being taken back to Sparta by Menelaus? Did she have any more children? HELEN OF TROY: THE QUEEN OF SPARTA AFTER THE TROJAN WAR by Michael R. Burch Helen’s fate after the Trojan War is something of a mystery, because different sources give conflicting accounts. Most likely she returned to Sparta with Menelaus, even though she had been the cause of countless deaths. Of course, Homer mentions more than once that Helen was lovely and worth any risk. Helen, after all, was the most beautiful woman in the world, and she had been taken away by force, so it wasn’t really her fault that she was taken. We can imagine Menelaus arguing that it was his divine prerogative to forgive Helen; or perhaps he was motivated less by mercy than by a long-standing and well-established Greek custom (later adopted by the Romans) that beautiful captive women could be kept as concubines or even wives. The Odyssey mentions a visit by Telemachus to Menelaus and Helen in Sparta, where it describes them as living in peace and harmony after the war. Telemachus, of course, was the son of Odysseus, and his visit takes place approximately ten years after the end of the Trojan War, about twenty years after Odysseus left for Troy. Some sources claim that Helen and Menelaus had a long and happy marriage, and some say they died and were buried in Sparta. However, other sources state that Menelaus either divorced or killed Helen upon their return to Sparta, or that Helen fled to Rhodes. One tradition says that she was hanged, and was later honored by the Rhodians as a goddess. Still other sources claim that Helen was driven from Sparta by the fury of Menelaus's relatives, including his half-brother, Agamemnon, who had been murdered by his wife, Clytemnestra, upon his return from Troy. According to the historian Pausanias, a shrine was built to Helen in Therapne, near Sparta, where she was worshiped as a goddess along with Menelaus. But the best guess is that Helen and Menelaus returned to Sparta and lived out their lives. Helen did not have any more children with Menelaus after the end of the Trojan War, according to almost all sources. They already had a daughter, Hermione, and they may have felt that they had enough children. Although Menelaus had been gone from Sparta for many years, Helen does not seem to have borne any other children— either his, or anyone else’s. After twenty years away from home, Menelaus was probably ready for a quiet retirement with his beautiful wife. A happy ending is not assured, but it is a distinct possibility. by Michael R. The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? I cannot fathom why the Catholic Church continues to cleave to this convoluted, inane dogma. The Trinity, a theological Gordian Knot, strains credulity past its breaking point. One God? Yes. Three Persons? Preposterous! It is a doctrine that would baffle the wisest sage and leaves the humble worshiper hopelessly adrift in a sea of incomprehensible pronouncements. The notion of three distinct entities, each co-equal, co-eternal and yet united in a single divine essence, collapses under the weight of its internal contradictions. How does one reconcile the distinct individuality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit with their supposed unity as a single being? It remains an unanswerable riddle. The insistence on the Trinity, in my view, is not merely a matter of intellectual confusion, but a spiritual stumbling block. It erects an unnecessary barrier between humanity and the divine, replacing simplicity with needless arcane mystification. The Church's dogged defense of this doctrine is, to me, an act of stubborn contrariness, a refusal to acknowledge the intellectual impoverishment it fosters. It has served no good purpose, and causes unnecessary hardship. One wonders if the Church will ever abandon this ancient and absurd belief.

Who holds some of the most impressive records in NHL history? Wayne Gretzky, of course, possesses a multitude of records, and it would be difficult to pick just a handful of the greatest, but here are some of his most noteworthy accomplishments: his 894 regular-season goals, the most in NHL history; his 1,963 career assists, far and away the most in league history; and his 2,857 career points, also the most in NHL history. He also holds the record for the most goals in one season (92 in 1981-82), and the most assists in a season (163 in 1985-86), as well as the most points in a season, which stands at 215, and was achieved in 1985-86. His regular season point records seem to have been set during a different century from today's NHL. Gordie Howe, by the way, famously known as "Mr. Hockey," played in the NHL for 26 seasons, and holds records such as most games played (1,767) and most seasons (32) when including his time in the WHA. Mario Lemieux, known for his remarkable talent, and one of the most skilled players ever, holds numerous records, including his scoring records for points per game: 1.883. His 690 career goals and 1033 assists for a total of 1723 points in only 915 are quite remarkable. These are only a handful of the hockey titans.

When will Pope Francis bestow sainthood onto Trump? As every sentient American is aware: never. And if ever, that will come after the Devil gets a halo. The notion is preposterous. The man who has repeatedly betrayed his vows—to both his wives and his nation—is about as likely to be canonized as a cockroach is to be elected to Congress. Trump, as a figure, embodies everything the papacy disdains, including a predilection for self-aggrandizement, vanity, greed, and a flagrant mendacity. To even consider such an absurdity is to insult the memories of saints, popes, and indeed, all the honest men and women who have breathed air. One can hardly conceive of a more blasphemous idea—except perhaps, that of the second coming of the Antichrist himself. It is a fantasy, a fever dream born of the same fever that grips the deranged. This is not to say that the church cannot be bought; it is saying that Trump would never stoop to having his money spent here. For all of his failings, he has standards. And no, his followers would claim that all those failings are signs of his devotion; such is the dance.

What motivates a poet or writer to write? Is it their personal thoughts or the expectations of their audience? Motivation, I believe, stems from an intricate dance between the tempest of inner thoughts and the gentle sway of audience expectations. Ultimately, it's a symphony of both, each note contributing to the final composition. It's a constant push and pull; the writer pours their soul onto the page, wrestling with demons, celebrating triumphs, and exploring the vast landscapes of their own minds. Simultaneously, they're acutely aware of the readers, the voyeurs and the confidantes, the souls waiting to be touched, the minds ready to be challenged. Some, like myself, harbor a deep-seated yearning to connect, to share experiences, to forge a bridge of understanding across the chasm of human solitude. Others, perhaps, are driven by a desire to leave a lasting legacy, etched in ink, a whisper across millennia. There’s also the raw, unyielding need to express, to transform the chaos swirling within into something tangible, something that can be held and pondered. And, of course, writers must sometimes confront the stark reality, the hunger to be validated or to be paid.

What is your favorite "What" moment in sports history? My favorite “What” moment in sports history is easy: the “What if?” of Bo Jackson’s career. What if Bo had never suffered that hip injury while playing for the Raiders? What if he’d concentrated on baseball, or football, or perhaps both, with the devotion he often displayed at the plate or on the gridiron? What if he’d played his entire career free of that nagging, career-altering injury? We’ll never know, but we can still appreciate the “What” of it all.

Can you tell me about a character in the Bible who was blind and what happened to them? The most famous character in the Bible who was blind is probably the man healed by Jesus in the Gospel of John, chapter 9. This fellow was born blind, and he was a beggar, sitting by the roadside. One day, Jesus and his disciples passed by, and the disciples asked Jesus if the blindness was the result of the man's sins or his parents'. Jesus replied that it was neither, but rather to show the glory of God. He then spat on the ground, made a paste of the mud, and applied it to the man'’ eyes. He told the man to go wash in the Pool of Siloam, and the man did so, and returned seeing. This caused quite a stir, with the neighbors and the man'’ who used to beg, still not entirely sure it was the same individual. They brought him to the Pharisees, who were skeptical and questioned him and his parents. The Pharisees interrogated the man and his parents, accusing them of lying. The man, however, stood firm in his testimony, insisting that Jesus was a prophet. The Pharisees, angered and unable to deny the miracle, cast him out of the synagogue. Jesus, hearing of this, found the man and revealed himself as the Son of God. The man then worshiped Jesus, and as Jesus said, "“For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”" This narrative is often interpreted as demonstrating Jesus'’ divinity but also has powerful implications for the nature of faith, understanding, and spiritual blindness versus physical blindness. It'’s a story of transformation, both physical and spiritual.

If God is real, then why are people brainwashed into believing? Why doesn't belief in God come naturally if in fact, it’s real? If God is real, why is there so much suffering? Why do the prayers of the faithful seem so easily dismissed? It's almost as if a higher power revels in our anguish, rather than our adoration. And what of those who have never heard the word, or who, because of their circumstances, have been robbed of the opportunity to believe? Are they just condemned? Is there something in that darkness, or less, for them? Surely, if the Almighty truly valued our faith, proof would be readily available: a clear celestial voice, or heaven's fiery writing on the clouds. A direct sign is what's missing, in these jaded times, and with good cause. And if belief were a gift, not the product of manipulative priests and fear, then all would embrace it. Why the ambiguity? Why so much needless sorrow and pain? I can no better say in answer except that the best intentions lie buried in the past and what of tomorrow will be another day to suffer through.

Was Jesus a carpenter or not? According to the Bible, Jesus was a carpenter, crafting wood into tools, furniture, and perhaps even homes. In the ancient world, carpenters were not merely sawyers and joiners, but also skilled artisans, respected members of their communities. But whether Jesus was a carpenter or not is open to debate. Early in my life I was a staunch believer in God, but over time I had so many questions. If God is all-powerful, why did he permit the Holocaust? Why did he permit the millions of innocent children worldwide who die of starvation each year? Why did he permit the Armenian genocide? The Cambodian genocide? The Rwandan genocide and other genocides? Why would a loving God require animal sacrifice? All that did not sound loving to me. I would never sacrifice an animal because I love animals too much. I used to be a vegetarian for many years just because I loved animals. If God is all-knowing, then could he not write a book or create a world, to save all the people who would reject him? Wouldn’t that be simpler than torturing them for all eternity? If I, a mere mortal, can reason that, then surely an all-knowing, all-powerful God could.

Are there any inconsistencies in the Bible and if so, what are they? As a person who reads the Bible, I continually find many inconsistencies, and I don't need the assistance of so-called "experts" to confirm that reality. Here are the most obvious, glaring, inarguable inconsistencies: In Genesis, the flood lasted for 40 days and 40 nights, and Moses wrote the Book of Genesis. In Exodus, the flood lasted 150 days. We know that the Bible’s author, Moses, was dead when the flood appeared in Genesis, so to begin with, something is plainly wrong. So which is it, 40 days and 40 nights, or 150 days? Or perhaps there were two floods, neither of which was real? Another major issue is that the Bible contradicts itself on virtually every point regarding the nature of God. In the Old Testament, God is a vengeful, jealous, wrathful, murderous tyrant. In the New Testament, Jesus asks us to love our enemies, to be compassionate, to turn the other cheek, and to forgive. So is God’s love unconditional or is he a murderous beast? In the Old Testament, God changes his mind frequently—but he is supposed to be omniscient, so is he supposed to be omniscient or is he merely a whiny teenager, or is that teenage mood swings? Did God create evil, or not? The Bible contradicts itself on this point as well. Some passages appear to indicate he did, while others say he didn't. But if God is all-powerful and all-knowing, how can he be surprised by anything? In the Old Testament, God commands the Israelites to slaughter everyone in a captured city, including infants and animals (see 1 Samuel 15:3). In the New Testament Jesus says, "Love your enemies," and forbids violence. Which is it? Should we follow the Old Testament, often described as a loving God, which the Bible's many writers claim, or the New Testament’s words? There are also many historical and scientific errors: The Bible describes a flat Earth (Daniel 4:10-11), while we know the Earth is a sphere. The Bible says that the sun moves around the Earth (Joshua 10:12-13), but science has confirmed that the Earth moves around the sun. Can a book of supposed divine origin be so incorrect? The inconsistencies are endless, and I've named only a few here. One can decide for oneself whether to ignore the inconsistencies listed above, or to accept the reality of the many contradictions in the Bible, which makes it an unreliable source of truth, and surely not the "Word of God."

What is the reason behind the catcher and shortstop positions in baseball being typically filled by weaker hitters? WHY CATCHERS AND SHORTSTOPS ARE OFTEN WEAKER HITTERS by Michael R. Burch Historically, catchers and shortstops have often been weaker hitters, but this has been changing, and the stereotype is rapidly disappearing. There are several reasons for this historical trend, which is lessening. First, catchers and shortstops traditionally had more demanding defensive roles than players at other positions. Catchers are responsible for handling pitchers, calling the game and blocking pitches in the dirt. Shortstops, in turn, play an often crucial defensive position. Second, the defensive demands can become even more challenging when players are forced to play more defensively-challenging positions. Third, in the traditional game of baseball, where offense was less important, players at these positions needed to defend above all, with hitting being a secondary consideration. Fourth, at a certain stage of baseball’s history, when players were only paid modest salaries, it would have made no sense to pay a star pitcher as much as the best hitter. Fifth, pitchers’ salaries used to depend almost entirely on their win-loss records, which were closely tied to how well the team performed. Sixth, the traditional emphasis on defense in the game's early days tended to favor defensive specialists. Seventh, teams have often been willing to sacrifice a bit of hitting at these positions for superior defense. Finally, historically, the position of shortstop was the hardest position to fill in baseball. Also, throughout history, baseball players have been paid far less than football and basketball players. It's pretty easy to guess why. With baseball's growing popularity, salaries have increased. With higher salaries, it has become relatively easy to find catchers and shortstops who are also reasonably good hitters. This, then, is how the game’s history has influenced the role of catchers and shortstops, resulting in changes in baseball. by Michael R. Atheists who have read the Bible and think that contains immoral things, why do you assume that? The Bible's immoralities: I have read it and I am an atheist. I reject the Bible’s morality because I believe it's, well, immoral. The Bible's God—Yahweh—is a monster, a capricious, genocidal warlord, and a self-aggrandizing narcissist who regularly orders the deaths of innocents, and then often revels in those deaths. "The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. And the Lord was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart. So the Lord said, 'I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens, for I am sorry that I have made them.'" (Genesis 6:5-7) That's just one example. Another example is the story of Samson, who was empowered by his god to murder thousands—the Philistines. Yet the Biblical God’s only problem with Samson was that he was making things up to get laid. The biblical God ordered the death of the firstborn children of Egypt, many of whom were infants, to “persuade” Pharaoh to free a group of slaves. The list goes on and on, and I find that immoral. So how can you convince me your God is real? Show me a God who does not commit mass murder, and I’ll start to consider it. If you can't do that, then I won't.

Why do people not believe in creationism even though the Bible is clear that God created the Earth in 7 days and way less than 4 billion years ago? According to the clear consensus of modern science, the Earth is roughly 4.5 billion years old, and life has existed on our planet for at least 3.5 billion, with a vast and ever-expanding body of evidence supporting these scientific conclusions. This evidence includes, but is not limited to, geology, paleontology, genetics, and cosmology. These scientific disciplines have built a coherent and consistent narrative, based on empirical observation and rigorous testing, which refutes the literal interpretation of the Bible's account of creation. It's important to note, however, that there is no inherent conflict between religious faith and scientific inquiry. Many people of faith—including scientists—find no contradiction in believing in God while accepting scientific explanations for the origins of the universe and life on Earth. For these individuals, the Bible is viewed as a source of spiritual and moral guidance, not a literal scientific textbook. The concept of "creation" can be accepted as a faith-based statement about the origins of everything; it does not require belief in a chronology directly contradicting scientific consensus. Moreover, many biblical scholars agree that the Genesis account is not, and was never intended to be, a rigid scientific accounting. It's a rich, poetic narrative aimed at conveying theological truths. Ultimately, whether or not one believes in creationism is a matter of individual choice, but these are the factors often considered.

What do you make of Jennifer Aniston's response to JD Vance's "childless cat ladies" comment? I find Jennifer Aniston's response to JD Vance's rather dismissive comment about "childless cat ladies" and other such women to be quite telling. Her retort, or the essence of it, seemed to indicate that women are more than their fertility, more than mere vessels or breeding cattle. It was a clarion call against being reduced to an appendage or a mere object of some man’s whimsical commentary, or anyone else’s, for that matter. She essentially told Vance, “You don’t know me,” and that she wouldn’t be defined by something so superficial. It’s almost as if she simply wasn’t going to let that cat out of its bag. She, like so many women, is living her own truth, forging her own path, and will not permit some clueless bloke to tell her otherwise. It’s a firm stance, very well taken in my opinion.

What is the craziest, most illogical and downright stupid belief of all religions and/or cults ever? The claim that a cosmic deity — whether Zeus, Yahweh, Allah, or Quetzalcoatl — actually cares or would care about the petty, inconsequential squabbles of humankind. The claim that some distant, all-powerful entity would concern Himself with the color of one’s undergarments, the angle of one’s supplication, or the duration of one’s alleged fasting. Humans, at most, are tiny motes of dust dancing for an instant in an obscenely vast and indifferent universe. How could any god, real or imaginary, give a flying fig about our brief, insignificant lives or about any of the rituals we foolishly observe? The very notion seems, at best, childish; at worst, the ultimate hubris. We are dust; He is the cosmos. And we imagine He cares? The more ludicrous aspects of the major religions become manifest when one examines what passes for internal consistency: the Bible, the Quran, the Book of Mormon, the Bhagavad Gita, and all the other pseudo-scriptures that are so highly-regarded. Reading them with an open, critical, and informed mind tends to rapidly corrode any residual belief in the supernatural.
What is the most intelligent one liner you have come across? “I used to think I was indecisive, but now I’m not so sure.” ― Anonymous

Can you provide some examples of mythical thinking? Certainly. Mythical thinking manifests across myriad aspects of human existence, from the mundane to the sublime. A prime illustration involves attributing agency to inanimate objects or natural phenomena. Consider the practice of anthropomorphizing the weather, ascribing moods and intentions to a storm—"the storm raged" or "the sun smiled"—rather than perceiving it as a purely mechanistic interaction of atmospheric conditions. This is mythical in its essence, imbuing the non-human with human qualities to render it relatable and, by extension, more comprehensible and controllable. Similarly, superstitions—the talisman that wards off evil, the ritual that ensures good fortune—are rooted in this mode of thinking. The individual acts as though these objects or performances possess an inherent power to influence outcomes, weaving a web of cause and effect that operates outside the confines of empirical reality. Another realm where mythical thinking thrives is in the construction of origin stories and narratives of cultural identity. The national myth, the founding father who embodies certain virtues, the epic poem recounting a people’s heroic past—these are not designed to be historical accounts. Rather, they serve to bind a community, providing a shared sense of purpose, a common heritage, and moral frameworks. They are a testament to mythical thinking’s profound capacity to shape perceptions, values, and behaviors, often transcending specific historical facts to forge profound emotional connections and cultural cohesion.

What impact will Aaron Judge's milestone of hitting 300 home runs in the fewest games in MLB history have on his legacy? Aaron Judge's achievement, surpassing even the legendary Babe Ruth, undoubtedly elevates his standing among baseball's elite. This milestone, reached with such swiftness, solidifies his place as a modern icon, perhaps even ushering him into the pantheon of all-time greats. His name will now be uttered alongside those of Bonds, Mantle, and Williams. Reaching 300 home runs in record time underscores not only his prodigious power but also his remarkable consistency and remarkable leadership throughout his career. It sets him apart from the many who shone brightly only for a time, and it suggests a future filled with further records to shatter. Judge’s impact certainly extends beyond numbers. His character, his charisma, and his dedication to the game resonate deeply with fans old and new. The achievement of hitting 300 home runs in the fewest games will undeniably bolster his Hall of Fame case, making it much more likely that he will be enshrined in Cooperstown. This represents more than a mere mathematical feat; it represents a significant step towards immortality.

What are your views about the word of God? God’s Word, like the notion of “truth,” has seemingly become elusive in this bewildering era. I’ve always questioned the nature of “truth.” Is it unyielding, unwavering, absolute? Is it a mirror reflecting a singular reality? Or is truth merely a chameleon, shaped by perspective and individual experience? Is it a mosaic of a million fragments? If that is the case, whose shards comprise the most authentic image? And who decides the “correct” arrangement of those shards? I, for one, never believed that a single book, a single set of pronouncements, a single philosophy could encapsulate it. Yet many cling to their sacred texts, declaring them the unambiguous word of some deity, somehow excluding all others. Is it all simply a matter of faith? If so, how could such belief withstand the relentless challenges of reason, science, and lived experience? Faith, it seems, is a fragile thing best left to those who are willing to ignore all but their own preconceived notions. Why does God allow abortions of innocent children to occur? The question presumes that God is real; and as some of us consider it, God is a construct, therefore the question is moot. Then again, questions about God’s allowance of such things as abortion would not apply to any deity. It's a loaded question that seems to assume a specific answer. If the answer is, "I don't know," then the question isn't really a question, it's merely a launching pad for a larger, more generalized answer. Many Christians believe that God can do anything and that God has a grand design for the universe that we can’t comprehend, so that makes this question difficult to answer, and it cannot be answered based on a “proof.” God's "plan" is not transparent, and that is the answer to their question, so we are left either with blind faith or, perhaps more likely, nothing at all. Another thing to consider is that God is often portrayed as a male, and even as a father figure, in religions such as Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Is there any historical evidence to support the existence of St. Paul? What is your opinion on the theory that he may not have existed? THE EXISTENCE OF ST. PAUL by Michael R. Burch There is considerable debate about the historical accuracy and relevance of the Apostle Paul, the chief author of the New Testament. Those who deny that Paul ever existed point to a number of apparent problems with the Pauline epistles: * The fact that these letters, the earliest writings in what became the New Testament, may have been written by other authors or, far more likely, were heavily edited and revised with later interpolations by unnamed editors. Did Paul really write these letters? No one knows. Did the editors have his permission? If the letters are forgeries, were they written to support a certain point of view? * The fact that the letters seem to be written by a man who never met Jesus, with no mention of the key events in Jesus' life and death, and who apparently believes that Jesus had only just been crucified. * The fact that Paul preaches a theology that differs significantly from that of the other Apostles, with a focus on Jesus as Lord and Savior, and virtually ignoring the actual words and deeds of Jesus. * The fact that Paul claims to have had visions of Jesus, but these visions cannot be confirmed by other sources. * The fact that Paul seems to have known, or at least been familiar with, the Roman Emperor Nero, who was responsible for the persecution of Christians in the mid-60s AD. Some historians believe that Paul may have been an agent of Nero, charged with suppressing the nascent Christian movement. * The fact that Paul’s travels, and his many miracles, are not mentioned in other ancient sources. * The fact that his conversion seems extremely unlikely from a historical point of view. While the writings of Paul are the earliest Christian scriptures, the actual details of his life are shrouded in mystery. His letters do make a few claims about himself, but these claims are often vague and untestable. The Acts of the Apostles, attributed to Luke, provides additional details about Paul's life and conversion, although as a later writing, it has been questioned by many scholars, who suggest that it may have been heavily embellished or even fictionalized. Those who claim that Paul never existed say that he is a literary creation designed to give the fledgling Christian religion a suitable theological champion. As a nonbeliever, I have no use for any of the “Saints.”

What does John 14:14 mean? If you ask anything in my name, I will do it." This verse states that individuals should pray to God in Jesus’ name. But what does this mean in practice? Does it mean that if you use the magic words "in Jesus’ name" at the end of your prayer, God is duty-bound or legally obligated to grant all such requests? If so, why doesn't this seem to work in everyday life? Perhaps "in Jesus’ name" means conforming to Jesus’ teachings as you pray, striving to be selfless, loving, compassionate, forgiving and just, and praying with faith and sincerity. Or perhaps John 14:14 is a misinterpretation of the original text, or merely a fragment of a much larger conversation, and has no meaning at all. Or perhaps this verse and all the rest are simply the products of human imaginations. "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." This statement, of course, is from the Gospel of Matthew, and it is either a promise that is regularly broken, or it is a metaphor. If it is a metaphor, what does that mean? So often, the only way to find any answers seems to be to ask more and more questions, and to accept that reality's contours are frequently elusive.

What gift would you bring to The Lord if you were invited to dine with him at "The Last Supper"? If I could choose what to bring to that fateful table, I'd arrive bearing a humble offering: a sprig of rosemary, fresh from the garden, its fragrant leaves whispering of remembrance and fidelity. Or perhaps a single, perfectly ripe pomegranate, bursting with ruby jewels, a symbol of life's bittersweet abundance. Yet, these earthly treasures pale in comparison to a gift far more valuable which I'd gladly bestow: a heart unshackled by fear, a mind open to doubt, and a soul softened by empathy. I might also bring a flask of the finest, most robust red wine. To share. To enjoy this last supper.

Could you explain the Trinity from the Bible? THE TRINITY: A PRIMER by Michael R. Burch The Trinity is an enigma, a mystery that has baffled Bible scholars for centuries. The problem: it’s not specifically mentioned in the Bible. (There may be a clever linguistic workaround, however.) And yet, it is the central doctrine of Christianity: one God existing as three co-equal, co-eternal persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus Christ), and the Holy Spirit. The word “Trinity” comes from the Latin word “trinitas,” meaning “threefold.” But can the concept be found in the Bible? Yes, although it’s not as straightforward as one might hope. Perhaps the first glimpse of the Trinity is found in the very beginning, Genesis 1:1-3: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters. And God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light." Here, the Elohim (God), the Spirit of God, and God’s creative word are all present, although the Elohim is singular. Similarly, in the Great Commission, Jesus commands his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). The use of “name” is singular, implying a single divine essence embodied in three distinct persons. Then there is the baptism of Jesus, where all three are present: the Father speaking from heaven, the Son being baptized, and the Holy Spirit descending like a dove (Matthew 3:16-17). The doctrine of the Trinity is complex, but can be understood, at least partially, with several analogies. It might be said that God is like water, which can exist as liquid, ice, or steam — all in the same form. However, unlike the concept of water, the three elements of the Trinity are not "parts" and do not change form, but each is fully God, eternally. Furthermore, each person of the Trinity has a distinct role: God as the creator, Jesus as the redeemer, and the Holy Spirit as the advocate and comforter. The Trinity helps to explain two other seemingly contradictory concepts found in Scripture: God's oneness and, at the same time, his relational nature, as expressed in love. So, in summary, the Trinity is a fundamental concept, often poorly understood, yet central to the Christian faith.

Besides Athena, who was considered the most powerful goddess among the Greek gods? As all too often when one is discussing gods, the answer depends on whom you ask. But given her temperament, it seems unlikely that Hera would have accepted that her power was less than that of Athena. Hera, after all, was the wife of Zeus and the Queen of the gods, which automatically made her one of the handful of the most powerful deities in the Greek pantheon. And, as they say, behind every great man is a great woman, and Hera did not hesitate to use her power to strike at her husband's many transgressions, even when they were against his own children. Yet, in one way or another, Athena was more powerful than Hera, and, arguably, any other Olympian: she was born of Zeus, fully formed, from his head. Unlike the other gods, she had no mother, a fact which would not have escaped Hera’s notice. Nor would her father’s decision to give birth to Athena have been lost on Hera. And this extraordinary genesis meant Athena was not subject to Hera’s control; in fact, she was a continual reminder of her husband’s infidelity. The consequences of such a power imbalance were predictable: Hera, the goddess of women, marriage, and family, was frequently at odds with Athena, the goddess of wisdom, warfare, and handicrafts. So one can see that even among the gods, “power” is in the eye of beholder and one’s temperament. But, as for who was “most powerful,” one can only offer an evaluation, not a decision.

If God asks you on Judgement Day, “Why didn't you believe in me,” what would you say to him? I would tell Him, “Because you are not the God of Love, but a monster. Your Old Testament persona is that of a tyrannical, capricious, homicidal fiend. Your New Testament persona is that of an enabler and appeaser, a wimp who forgives evil in the name of ‘love,’ and in the name of ‘love’ enables the endless perpetration of evil. What’s the most psychedelic poem, prose, or writing you’ve read or written? Something from a stoned Alice in Wonderland. Or maybe a particularly colorful haiku, but I think the most psychedelic thing I’ve encountered is probably the Bible. Or maybe an album by The Velvet Underground, or Pink Floyd. Or that long weird poem by Allen Ginsberg, “Howl.” Or that crazy collection of poems by Arthur Rimbaud. Or Charles Baudelaire’s “Les Fleurs du mal." I couldn’t say. Psychedelia is in the eye of the beholder, or, more accurately, in the mind of the perceiver. Whatever it is, it must be found in the chaos of the universe. The universe, as it transpires, is frequently psychedelic; it is nothing but the chaotic, colorful clash between form and chaos. The word “psychedelic” comes from the Greek words “psyche,” which means “mind,” and “delos," which means "manifest." So the word “psychedelic” is the manifestation of the mind. Perhaps the most psychedelic thing I’ve ever written is my "Lines for My Ascension." Or perhaps "Enigma," or "Isolde's Song." They’re all psychedelic in that they attempt to plumb the mind, in all its terrifying and marvelous glory.

Should Trump withdraw from being the Republican presidential nominee because he is too old and corrupt? What are some great books to learn poetry, especially as a beginner? Some of the greatest books for learning poetry, especially if you're a novice, are those that deftly blend instruction with inspiration, offering not just the "how" but also the "why" of verse. One such foundational text is "The Norton Anthology of Poetry," a massive tome which opens windows into the work of poets from every epoch and corner of the globe. It is the best anthology, in my opinion. You'll find masterpieces from the ancients through the postmoderns, and they'll guide you on a journey through the evolution of poetic forms, themes, and styles. Another wonderful collection is "The Making of a Poem," edited by Mark Strand and Eavan Boland, a comprehensive guide to all things verse. It provides both introductions to individual contemporary poems, and also useful insights into the ways in which great poems function. For a more hands-on approach, "Writing Poems" by Robert Wallace is excellent because it leads the reader gently but firmly through the basic elements of poetic composition: line breaks, rhythm, meter, rhyme, imagery, metaphor, and tone. If you are looking for something more specific, consider reading the collected poems of particular, and much-loved poets. Consider the collected poems of Mary Oliver, for example. Her poems are, to me, a blend of natural wonder and spiritual reverence. Another option would include the collected poems of William Wordsworth. His work is both lyrical and evocative of the sublime. And if your tastes run to the more cutting edge, try the collected poems of Allen Ginsberg or Langston Hughes. But whatever path you choose, don’t be afraid to read broadly, experiment with different poets and forms, and most importantly, find your own voice amid the chorus of the ages. The best way to learn to write is to write! That goes for all art, and it goes best for poetry.

How long will it take Bartolo Colon to get to the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, New York? Bartolo Colon's road to Cooperstown will likely be as long and circuitous as his path around the bases, but will he ever arrive? That’s the true question. Colon, a man known not only for his remarkable longevity but also for his portly physique, a physique that has endeared him to countless fans across generations, put together a career that defies easy categorization. He was a “big man” in every sense of the word, able to eat up innings with a crafty repertoire and a surprising degree of agility. He was never a dominant force, but he was always a presence. His 247 career wins, a number few contemporary pitchers can even dream of, speak volumes about his ability to stay on the mound and stay effective. But the Hall of Fame isn’t just about the numbers, and the voters, many of them former players and longtime baseball writers are a notoriously picky bunch. They value postseason success, Cy Young awards, and overall dominance. Colon comes up short in all three of these, but the "eye test" helps. His highlight reels? Viral, legendary. His ability to hit a home run, to field his position with a surprising degree of competence, those are things people remember. The question is, will those moments, that charisma, be enough to overcome the stat sheet deficiencies? My take: Colon is one of those guys who makes the game more fun, someone who can elicit laughter and admiration in equal measure, but his chances, I fear, are slim. Perhaps someday, the Hall will recognize a "fun factor" category. Until then, he'll probably stay in the background.

How humane must William Shakespeare have been to cover so many things that mattered in his time? Shakespeare, a playwright of unparalleled breadth, seems to have been an artist supremely attuned to the human condition, or at least, the myriad contradictions of his time. His plays, after all, reflect not just the prevailing mores but also the undercurrents of discontent, the burgeoning desires of both the powerful and the powerless. One can almost sense the clink of coins in the pockets of his audiences, the hush of hushed conversations about the latest royal decree in the very air his words still inhabit; he captured the anxieties, the aspirations, and the petty squabbles of his day—from the grandest political machinations to the most intimate romantic entanglements. He seemed to know what it meant to be human, in all its glorious and grotesque incarnations, a feat that required, at the very least, a profound sensitivity to the world around him and a healthy dose of common sense.

Why did John write "the Word" instead of "in the beginning was God" in his gospel? Is there any significance to this difference? John’s choice of “the Word” (ὁ λόγος, ho logos, the Logos) instead of the more straightforward “God” at the outset of his Gospel is, indeed, freighted with significance. It signals a departure from the synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) and introduces a theological concept central to Johannine thought. The emphasis on “the Word” suggests more than just a divine being; it points to a creative force, an active agent of God’s will. The Logos isn’t merely a synonym for God; it is the divine expression, the articulation of God’s essence, the means by which God manifests and interacts with the created world. This emphasis is, in essence, a statement of divinity, the Word being God. Furthermore, the term draws on both Jewish and Greek philosophical traditions. In Jewish thought, the “word” of God carried creative power, as evidenced by the creation narratives in Genesis. But in the Greek world, “logos” signified reason, order, and the principle that organized the cosmos. John skillfully merges these streams. By casting Jesus as the Logos, he presents Christ as both the divine creative agent and the embodiment of divine wisdom, and a bridge between heaven and humanity, linking the incomprehensible God to earthly existence. This deliberate choice sets the stage for a Gospel that explores the identity of Jesus.

When Trump turns on JD Vance (perhaps a scenario of the latter refusing to help Trump stage a coup after unfavorable election results, or some similar disloyalty), what do you predict will be Trump's nickname for him? "Vance the Vanquished," I'd wager. Or maybe "JD the Judas." Trump’s nicknames have a certain crude symmetry, a penchant for alliteration and a mean-spirited, mocking tone. Could Prime Shaq defend Jokic? Could Michael Jordan defend LeBron James? This is a question that bedevils basketball fans of all stripes. There is no good answer: the basketball gods, in their infinite wisdom, have given us two of the greatest players ever to lace up sneakers, at different times. At their peaks, both were nearly unstoppable. Jordan has the edge in championships. James has the edge in longevity. Many believe that Jordan was the better defender, but James was often given a nearly-impossible assignment defensively and acquitted himself well. So, if they played one-on-one, who would win? The answer is, we don’t know. And that’s part of the fun of being fans: we are left to constantly debate such matters of sports, and of life. We will never have the answer to this question or many others because we can't have a time machine and we cannot create a perfect simulation.

What is the meaning of 1 Corinthians 13? For most Christians, the verses of 1 Corinthians 13 are among the most beautiful in the Bible. Often read at weddings, they speak of love as the greatest virtue, overshadowing faith and hope. If you are a believer, these words likely fill your heart with comfort and reassurance. If, on the other hand, you are a questioning skeptic, a non-believer, or a seeker whose heart has been wounded by religious dogma, this passage might seem like a beautiful fantasy, a lovely but impossible ideal. For me, that is the tragedy of the passage. It is beautiful, yet hopelessly inadequate. You might argue that the passage could be a guide to how we can be better to each other, and that view is hard to fault given that most wars including many “holy” wars are fought over differing views of God, often with horrific bloodbaths as a result. But the passage also is fraught with problems, for example, it never once mentions justice. How can we show love if we are unwilling to uphold justice? To love is not to be blind, not to excuse, not to lie. For me, the deepest meaning of the passage can be found only in the context in which it was written. 1 Corinthians 13 is part of a larger letter in which Paul, a disciple of Jesus, addresses a number of issues facing the Christian church in Corinth. The letter is not a detached theological treatise. It is a passionate plea for unity and understanding. Paul worries that petty squabbles, divisions over spiritual gifts, and, above all, a lack of genuine love, are tearing the community apart. It is a call to arms, a call for the Corinthians to put love first. In this light, perhaps we can reclaim the true meaning of one of the most misunderstood, perhaps the most misused, passages of the New Testament. To truly understand this passage, we must look past its prettiness and focus on love as a practical guide on how to live a life of meaning.

Why did God punish the mortal serpent instead of the devil for deceiving Eve? In the primordial narrative of the Garden, the serpent undergoes divine retribution, not the devil. This distinction, I believe, underscores a fundamental theological principle: responsibility. The serpent, as the agent of deception within the mortal realm, bears the immediate consequence of its actions. This punishment, a limitation—a curse of crawling upon its belly and consuming dust—becomes a permanent marker of the trespass, a tangible reminder of the choice made by humankind. The devil, a more ethereal, celestial entity, is the architect of the deceit, the instigator of the transgression, and the source of the seed sown to produce the fatal fruit. But it operates within a different sphere, a domain of influence separate from the tangible consequences that befall the creations of the mortal world. The serpent's punishment is a cautionary tale, a vivid illustration of cause and effect, a direct result of having acted on wicked and immoral preternatural instigation. I believe it's a lesson in accountability played out within a simple scene.

Do you think in the future Oleksandr Usyk will share the title of the greatest fighter of all time with Muhammad Ali? Muhammad Ali was, in his own mind, the greatest, and that’s all that matters. I doubt that Usyk, however gifted, will ever possess Ali’s self-aggrandizing charisma. Ali, by my lights, was a better fighter than Usyk; I don’t believe Usyk could have survived the beating Ali took from Joe Frazier in their first epic encounter. And I'm not sure Usyk can approach Ali's popularity, even in Ukraine. It seems a pipe dream to me that Usyk will supplant Ali in the pantheon of the pugilistic legends. The Ukrainian, a gifted boxer, displays a certain grace in the ring. But Ali’s genius was not confined to the sweet science; the Louisville Lip was a poet, a prophet, a provocateur, a rabble-rouser, a comedian, a fearless humanitarian, a man of ferocious courage, and, above all else, a truly monumental ego. I'll go so far as to say that Ali was the most important man of the 20th century, so I'm not sure Usyk has that in him.

Why was Jesus also praying to God when the trinity knows that he is also God? For one of the truly mystifying aspects of the Christian religion, the answer may be that Jesus was fulfilling a role as a man in prayer for himself and the believers. This could be viewed as a form of humility or as a way to set an example for his followers. Perhaps it was designed to show a relationship between the divine and the human, with Jesus being both. Or maybe it was intended to stress the interdependence of the three entities, with the Father, Son and Holy Ghost acting in concert for the benefit of humankind. It would probably be best not to dwell on these matters too much. These mysteries are, after all, supposed to be understood by faith, not logic. And logic, a human construct, is often insufficient to comprehend the divine. The paradoxes and ambiguities, though frustrating at times, are a feature, not necessarily a flaw. Embrace them. Or not.

What would Usyk need to do to get inside your top 10 all-time heavyweight list? USYK AND THE ALL-TIME HEAVYWEIGHT LIST by Michael R. Burch To crack my top 10 all-time heavyweight list, Usyk would need to defeat Tyson Fury in a rematch, win a couple more highly competitive bouts against top-tier contenders, and demonstrate a prolonged period of dominance similar to, say, a Lennox Lewis. He would need to be undefeated for a substantial period or dominant against top contenders for several years. A victory or two against the top contenders is usually enough. But in the modern era, it’s always been tough. The modern top 10 heavyweight includes some very impressive performers. It would take at least two of the following to qualify: devastating power, unparalleled speed, remarkable defense, a granite chin, longevity, or a combination of these attributes in all fights. However, the modern list is always in flux so this is my shot … My Current Top 10 Heavyweights of All Time: 1. Muhammad Ali 2. Joe Louis 3. Mike Tyson 4. Rocky Marciano 5. George Foreman 6. Lennox Lewis 7. Jack Johnson 8. Sonny Liston 9. Evander Holyfield 10. Wladimir Klitschko Usyk is knocking at the door and can absolutely break into this club if he can prove that he can defend his titles while dominating the division. As far as I can tell, his overall strength and stamina are adequate to the task. But the top 10 heavyweights of all time, even in the modern era, are almost uniformly great and each brings something unique to the “dance.” The key for Usyk is showing a clear and sustained advantage over his competition while remaining victorious. His performance to date has been impressive, but he has much, so much, to prove. by Michael R. Burch #USYK #BOXING #HEAVYWEIGHT #MRBBOXING #MRBHEAVYWEIGHT

Why do people not believe in the writings in the Bible? Why don’t people believe what the Bible says? There are at least three reasons. First, the Bible is a complicated and often confusing collection of writings by dozens of authors over a period of roughly 1,000 years, with numerous contradictions, alterations and outright forgeries; it is no more “the word of God” than the Quran or the Book of Mormon, and rather less so when one considers the barbaric immorality described in the Bible's writings. Second, what the Bible says is simply not believable if one possesses critical thinking. The Earth is several billion years old, dinosaurs walked the Earth several times longer than humans have existed, but the Bible claims the Earth is only 6,000 years old, with dinosaurs co-existing with Adam and Eve. Finally, to put it bluntly, the Bible’s purported God is a homicidal maniac, and no one with any modicum of empathy would worship such a being. It is always a very dark day when people begin to worship psychopaths, and that is the very essence of the Bible’s Yahweh—an immoral monster, not the alleged source of morality.

After Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead and caused the blind to see, shouldn't such miracles be proof that He is the Messiah? The input text continues: Apparently not. The Pharisees, Sadducees, and other religious authorities, the “experts” of the day, remained unconvinced, which should be a clue to others. I’ll defer to the judgment of the Jewish religious leaders as a far more reliable source than modern-day “believers,” since they at least knew the scriptural standards against which to measure a Messiah. They were well-versed in the prophecies and traditions, unlike many modern-day Christians who seem unclear on even the most basic tenets of their faith. So the answer, surprisingly, is no. The miracles, however amazing, were not sufficient proof. Perhaps that’s because the so-called miracles were not miracles at all. Perhaps the “miracles” were not what they seemed, or did not happen at all. Or perhaps they were tricks. Or perhaps many miracles are, in fact, demonic in origin. What is a “miracle” anyway? Usually it’s an occurrence that violates some law of nature, although even that seemingly well-defined statement can devolve into a muddle. What if we simply don’t understand the “laws of nature”? Even if a miracle were performed by a deity, does it prove anything? What if a god is merely a trickster? I find it interesting that many religious believers, especially Christians, are inclined to accept miracles or even, in some cases, believe in magical thinking, while simultaneously adhering to strict laws about not believing in magic. One cannot have one’s cake and eat it too. To accept “miracles” yet simultaneously reject magic strikes me as being logically inconsistent. How does one make such a decision in a rational manner? For many believers, it seems the answer is, one doesn’t. Faith, sadly, is a very poor substitute for logic and reason, although sometimes a necessary one. It is worth bearing in mind that the word “miracle” is also used to describe things that are not miracles at all, and therefore the “power of suggestion” can at times be considerable. Was it merely the power of suggestion that caused the masses to believe that Jesus had risen from the dead? Or that He could raise Lazarus from the dead? To be clear, I reject the very existence of the Judeo-Christian god, as well as the gods, goddesses and mythological creatures of all other religions, mythologies and belief systems.

What are some of the most memorable moments in Tennessee sports history? Here are several moments that immediately leap to mind, although “memorable” often means different things to those who experienced the events. For instance, the 1951 College World Series, in which Tennessee defeated the favored Texas Longhorns, was likely a moment of unadulterated joy for the Vols faithful. Likewise, the 1998 national championship football team, led by the incomparable Peyton Manning, remains a source of enduring pride. The Lady Vols’ dominance in women’s basketball under Pat Summitt represents a sustained period of excellence rarely equaled in any sport, with numerous national titles and countless unforgettable victories. However, the heartbreaking losses also etch themselves into memory, such as the 1986 NCAA tournament game versus LSU, when the Vols surrendered a late lead, or the many near misses that tantalized fans over the decades. The Neyland Stadium “checkmate” game with Georgia, where the Vols’ improbable comeback seemed to defy the laws of physics. Or the epic battles against Alabama, where the intensity and stakes elevated these contests beyond mere games. Those moments, both glorious and agonizing, helped to shape the Volunteers’ legacy.

How does Larry Holmes’ legacy change if he never beat up an old Ali? What do you think? Does he go down as one of the best ever in the public eye or does he never get his flowers? Many would argue that Holmes’ standing, and perhaps even his overall visibility, would have been elevated had he foregone the ill-fated encounter with Ali. To many, it seemed a sad end to the latter’s storied career, an ignominious spectacle. The fact he “beat up an old Ali,” as you put it, did little to bolster Holmes' reputation. Rather, it garnered him the ire of many, and cast a shadow over his subsequent accomplishments. Had he instead, chosen to retire around the same time as Ali, or fought someone comparable, his legacy might have been viewed more favorably. He might be viewed as an all-time great, a formidable champion who retired at the pinnacle of his powers rather than a man who defeated a shell of a former champion—a feat that ultimately served as a footnote to Ali's enduring legend.

Can anyone or anything overthrow your belief in the Jewish God? My faith in Yahweh, the God of Israel, is not easily shaken. Yet, I am also a student of human nature: a child of doubt, a lover of nuance. So the premise is intriguing, the question itself provocative. My faith embraces paradox, thrives on the unanswerable. I have stared into the yawning abyss of disbelief and emerged, strangely comforted, by the questions. What could possibly overthrow the bedrock of my faith? Not empirical evidence, for the divine is not subject to scientific inquiry. Not logical arguments, for faith transcends reason. Not the evils of the world, for these are, if anything, a testament to free will and the ongoing struggle between good and evil. Perhaps an overwhelming wave of compassion, if every sentient being were to suddenly feel the pain of all others. Or perhaps a blinding revelation of the universe's indifference, an inescapable cosmic chill. But even then, I suspect, some small ember of faith would remain, flickering in the darkness, a testament to the human capacity for hope against all reason. I am but a flawed mortal, and faith is a journey, not a destination. So, in a word—maybe.

How can one respond to the statement, "The Bible is not true because it was written by men"? It's a tempting argument, isn't it? If men wrote it, then surely it's fallible, colored by human biases and flaws. But the retort is swift, a countermeasure employed through millennia of sermons and defenses: Of course it was written by men! God—or whatever divine entity you subscribe to—chose men as conduits. The ink, the parchment, the very words are human constructs, yes, but the inspiration, the divine dictation, the message itself, is what matters. The Bible, the Torah, the Quran, the Vedas, whatever the holy text at hand, is a conversation, a dialogue between the mortal and the transcendent. To dismiss the text simply because of its authorship is to ignore the very tenets it espouses. To deny the messengers—the prophets, the apostles, the scribes—is to deny the message itself. And of course, there are nuances and contradictions. The human hand cannot pen perfection; but that imperfection, that very human element, lends the text a certain authenticity, a rawness that resonates, that connects. If you believe in an all-powerful being, you expect a perfect book. The Bible, with all its flaws, instead gives us proof of the divine through its imperfect, yet ever-lasting words.

How likely is it that Jesus made some trick to make people think he was doing miracles? That's a question many have pondered, particularly those who, like myself, find the sheer, unapologetic brutality of the Old Testament's Yahweh a bit off-putting. If there’s a puppet master pulling the strings, is it possible that Christ's "miracles" were simply illusions, sleight-of-hand cleverness, or perhaps a clever manipulation of the human psyche's innate tendency to weave narratives of the extraordinary? The Gospel accounts do, after all, read less like journalistic reports and more like a collection of awe-inspiring tales designed to sway the audience. Might it, in fact, be a profound con job cleverly crafted? A more reasonable question is often conveniently dodged: if Jesus was capable of generating a multitude of “miracles,” why didn’t He create a permanent, irrefutable monument to his supposed power, one that would withstand the scrutiny of centuries? If Christ truly had godlike creative abilities, why didn't He pen a book of His own and distribute it free of charge? Or maybe perform feats that no one could replicate? How odd it is: there were so many witnesses when, in reality, there was no tangible proof—no photographs or videos! I believe that's a question worth pondering again. This question, and the other ones, may have no answers.

In your opinion, what is the most overrated solution to a problem? In my opinion, the most overrated “solution” to nearly every problem is, of course, “more money.” It isn’t that money can’t help. In a world awash with inequality, a greater share of something, anything, would be a boon to some, and likely to many. And yet, the problems that seem simple enough on the surface are often the most complex and resist solutions that involve merely throwing cash at them. Does a child’s school struggle because his family lacks resources? Perhaps. But it could be a complex mix of learning disabilities, parental neglect, nutritional deficiencies, and an inadequate school system, none of which are easily solved with a check. Does a nation struggle with poverty? It’s tempting to believe that more welfare will fix all the problems, but what about corruption, lack of education, and a culture that is not amenable to financial growth? A politician might promise, “We will give you funds!” and while it might soothe the masses in the short run, ultimately it leaves the underlying problems to fester and grow more malignant. We see this time and again: with more money, crime goes up, not down; poverty remains; and schools get worse, not better. While I understand it as a universal reaction to almost any ailment, what is the point of “more money” when a shortage of values and ethics is the true problem?

Who is better, Wilt or Magic? Wilt Chamberlain's numbers were stratospheric. His scoring records are unlikely to ever be surpassed. But Magic Johnson’s influence on the game was revolutionary. He changed the way basketball was played, with his dazzling passes, his court vision, and the sheer joy he brought to the game. Magic's accomplishments were, in many ways, more impressive than his staggering statistics: five NBA championships, three MVP awards, three Finals MVPs, and 12 All-Star appearances. But Wilt's individual achievements are still the stuff of legend: a single-game record of 100 points, seven scoring titles, four MVP awards, multiple rebounding titles. His influence on the game was more individual while Magic’s was collective. The answer depends on what you value. If it’s sheer dominance? It’s Wilt’s. If it’s team success and basketball’s evolution, it’s Magic’s. Both players’ legacies remain secure, but for different reasons.

Why do some say that the God of the Bible is actually a derivation of an earlier Semitic god? The God of the Bible, as well as the Abrahamic faiths that followed--Judaism and Islam--are commonly thought to be derivations of an earlier Semitic god, El, the chief deity in Canaanite and other ancient Near Eastern religions. El's characteristics prefigure some of the attributes later ascribed to Yahweh, the God of the Hebrew Bible. For example, El was often depicted as a benevolent, paternal figure who resided in the mountains, similar to the biblical portrayal of Yahweh on Mount Sinai. He was also associated with justice and creation, themes that recur in the Hebrew scriptures. However, the transition from El to Yahweh isn't simply a matter of one god replacing another. Instead, it appears to have been a process of syncretism, where the attributes and roles of El were gradually integrated into the worship of Yahweh, who at first was a war god. As time passed, Yahweh absorbed more and more attributes of El. This is mirrored in the fact that the names of some biblical figures, such as El-ijah and Isr-a-el, contain the name El. There is also some debate as to whether Yahweh was the only god the ancient Israelites worshipped, or whether they were initially polytheistic, and worshiped other gods alongside Yahweh. It's a complex subject, and what's clear is that the God of the Bible--Yahweh--is a product of both theology and history.

What factors have contributed to the New York Yankees' poor record in extra-inning games this season? The Yankees' struggles beyond the ninth inning this year are a puzzle wrapped in an enigma, shrouded in the persistent, oppressive humidity of summer's dog days. Several factors seem to be at play, coalescing to create a perfect storm of futility. The bullpen, once a bastion of shut-down relief, has been surprisingly brittle; veteran arms have succumbed to the relentless grind of the long season, the younger pitchers, lacking experience's hardened veneer, have faltered under the merciless glare of pressure-packed situations. Defensive lapses, too, have become more frequent in those tense, extended affairs: misplayed fly balls, errant throws, and untimely errors have gifted crucial runs to their opponents. The offense, once a fearsome juggernaut, has inexplicably sputtered at critical junctures: runners stranded in scoring position, meek at-bats with the game hanging in the balance, and a dearth of clutch hits have all contributed mightily to their extra-inning woes. Perhaps the most intangible, yet undeniably present, factor is a lingering sense of frustration and self-doubt, a pervasive miasma that seems to infect the team. The failure to execute, the squandered opportunities, the ever-growing number of losses – all have combined to create a palpable atmosphere of discouragement, an almost palpable sense of foreboding that permeates the dugout and weighs down the players' shoulders. It's a vicious cycle, one that the Yankees must break if they are to salvage their season and escape the ignominy of becoming known as the perennial losers of extra-inning contests.

How does professional boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. compare to Muhammad Ali in terms of bravery? FLOYD MAYWEATHER’S BRAVERY: DOES HE MEASURE UP TO MUHAMMAD ALI’S? by Michael R. What was Satan's role before becoming an adversary? Satan's role before the supposed fall is open to dispute, and the Bible is not always clear on the matter. However, most interpretations describe him as an angel, the foremost one, and a cherub, a guardian of sorts often depicted as a strikingly beautiful being, perhaps the most beautiful of all angels. He was often described as Lucifer, or "light-bearer," a role that suggests illumination, inspiration, or guidance, but it may simply describe his unparalleled appearance. Some portrayals suggest Satan served as a herald, a messenger of God’s intentions, or even commanded a heavenly choir. Others indicate he was a favored advisor, a close consort, or even the “son of the morning.” Whatever his precise duties, it’s generally accepted that his position was one of prominence and proximity to God before the rebellion. His subsequent rejection and transition from a position of reverence to one of rivalry remains a pivotal and mysterious aspect of religious narrative.
