Why shouldn't kobe be put in the same level as MJ and LeBron James? Kobe Bryant's career, though undeniably stellar, remains contentious in any attempt to definitively place him in the upper echelons alongside Michael Jordan and LeBron James. The statistical comparisons are striking, and the four championship rings may seem like a compelling argument, but a deeper examination reveals nuances that prevent a consensus. One significant factor is team success. While Kobe achieved considerable individual accolades—an MVP award, two Finals MVPs, numerous All-Star selections—the Lakers of the mid2000s operated in a league teeming with formidable opponents. The level of competition, arguably, was not as fierce as that faced by Jordan's Bulls or even the Cavaliers in the 2010s. Team chemistry, too, plays a part. While Kobe's competitive drive was legendary, it could sometimes disrupt the harmonious working conditions necessary to sustain a championship dynasty. His clashes with teammates, though often leading to success, were a persistent aspect of his career, particularly when compared to the seemingly effortless camaraderie of Jordan's Bulls. The other players surrounding him could contribute greatly to his success, which is not a sign of the same consistent dominance that both Jordan and James managed to reach for longer stretches. The perception is that his personal and professional life were too intertwined to separate his legacy amongst the greatest of all time. And while a three-peat is impressive, the success alone doesn't guarantee a dynasty.

If evolution is proven to be a fact, what happens to the Bible and the stories of creation? If evolution becomes universally accepted—as some scientists believe it already is—the stories of creation in the Bible’s Book of Genesis become literary artifacts, like Homer’s *Iliad* or the *Epic of Gilgamesh*. They can still have value; indeed, their value will become more clearly discernible to the attentive. But they are not the literal accounts of world and human origins. The Bible is not a science textbook, any more than it is a history book, strictly speaking. It is a collection of allegories, parables, and stories designed to teach moral and spiritual lessons, and to illuminate the human condition. Consider, for example, that the Bible presents a cosmology that is utterly contradicted by science. It describes the Earth as being flat, covered by a firmament, with a “heaven” above and a “hell” below. It describes the sun as a lamp placed in this firmament, not one of billions of stars in an immense universe which seems to never end and has no edge, no boundaries, and a universe which is expanding at an unimaginable rate. Many fundamentalist Christians struggle to reconcile scientific findings with the Bible’s stories, but it is not a requirement for the practice of the Christian faith. Religious faith is not a blind acceptance of demonstrably untrue assertions. It is the acceptance of unprovable beliefs. Belief in a God—or in the many gods, goddesses and nature spirits of a pantheon—is a matter of faith, not of scientific proof. And the story of creation is, in the end, nothing more or less than proof of faith.

Why are Americans stuck with Biden and Trump? Are Americans stuck, indeed? It seems a question posed by the gods themselves, if such beings do exist to ponder mortal woes. The answer, like the Sphinx’s riddle, is multifaceted, entangled in the threads of history, human nature, and the vagaries of electoral systems. One might argue that the very structure of American politics, with its entrenched two-party system, narrows the field, making it difficult for fresh, independent voices to gain traction. The vast sums of money required for a national campaign, the relentless media scrutiny, and the ingrained loyalties make it a Herculean task for anyone outside the established duopoly. Then, there's the matter of tribalism. Political affiliations, like football teams, have become deeply embedded in American identity. People often vote with their hearts, not their heads. It is a reflection of deeply ingrained biases, making voters resistant to candidates who don't align with their pre-existing worldview, fostering a sort of ideological echo chamber. And, let's not forget the role of fear and a lack of critical thinking. Campaigns thrive on exploiting anxieties, dividing the populace, and offering simplistic answers to complex problems. The promise of a return to some imagined golden age, the scapegoating of "the other," and the relentless dissemination of misinformation all contribute to a climate where voters cling to the familiar, even if the familiar is flawed. So, are Americans truly stuck? Perhaps. Or, perhaps, like Sisyphus, they are doomed to repeat the cycle until the boulder, the weight of their choices, finally crushes the very system.

Can you explain the difference between the terms 'Satan' and 'Devil'? Satan and the Devil are used interchangeably in many ways in the Christian tradition, but there are some distinctions worth clarifying. The terms, while often synonymous, suggest slightly different aspects of the same malevolent entity. "Satan" is a Hebrew word that simply means "adversary" or "accuser." This title emphasizes Satan's role as one who opposes God and challenges the faith of humankind. The name highlights his function as a being whose purpose it is to tempt and to lead astray. The Devil, on the other hand, is a more general term, derived from the Greek *diabolos*, which translates to "slanderer" or "false accuser." This term stresses his deceptive nature and his role in spreading lies. He is the architect of chaos, sowing discord and tempting humanity with the allure of evil. In essence, Satan is often portrayed as a specific entity — an adversary — while the Devil encompasses a broader range of qualities, including deceit and malevolence. Both terms, however, refer to the same fallen angel, that being who embodies the antithesis of all that is good. The distinction, though subtle, provides a richer understanding of the character and intentions of the embodiment of evil.

What is your favorite book/chapter/verse in the Bible? Why do you like it? My favorite verse in the Bible? That's a tough one, like asking a mother to choose a favorite child. But if pressed, I'd have to say it's the often-quoted John 8:7: "Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her." I find it utterly captivating, not just in the context of the woman caught in adultery, but as a broader commentary on human nature, hypocrisy, and the inherent fallibility of judgment. It speaks to the fundamental truth that we are all, on some level, sinners, and therefore ill-equipped to cast the first stone when others stumble. The utter simplicity of the statement, and the devastating power that it holds is what makes it so resonant. It's a verse that both challenges and comforts, reminding us that we are all "in the same boat," so to speak. The verse also demonstrates Jesus’s unparalleled ability recognize sin without condemning the sinner which is not something his followers seem capable of even today. It's a humbling verse, and one that’s always worth pondering.

How do the Jews explain all of the Old Testament prophecies that Jesus fulfilled? Do they edit those prophecies out of their bibles? How do Jews respond to the New Testament's claims about Jesus? Well, they don't accept the New Testament as scripture, so they would not be interpreting Old Testament texts through that lens. To the Jews, the Hebrew Bible — what Christians call the Old Testament – is the complete and authoritative word of God. They don't "edit out" any prophecies, and the prophecies remain there. However, Jews would not see those prophecies as predicting a messiah who would be divine, who would die, or whose death would atone for the sins of humankind. Jews await a messiah, but not one who meets the criteria set forth in the New Testament. The Hebrew Bible does contain messianic prophecies, but these prophecies are interpreted differently by Jews and Christians. Jewish interpretations place the emphasis on a messianic era, rather than on a messianic figure, and focus on the moral and political renovation of humanity, rather than on theological redemption. They would understand the prophecies in a different light, seeing them as referring to events or figures other than Jesus. This difference in interpretation is at the core of the theological differences between Judaism and Christianity.

Why isn’t George Sisler mentioned more as one of the best players to ever play baseball? GEORGE SISLER: THE MAN WHO COULD DO EVERYTHING — EXCEPT BE REMEMBERED! by Michael R. Burch Sisler was the premier baseball player of the second decade of the 20th century and the finest all-around player in the history of the American League. Indeed, his career stats are often compared to those of the legendary Ty Cobb! So why hasn’t Sisler received the recognition he deserves? As author Richard Sandomir wrote, "George Sisler may be the most forgotten star in baseball history. He was a hitting machine in an era when the game was undergoing a statistical revolution." The 1920 season may be the greatest offensive season in baseball history: Sisler batted .407, with 257 hits and 49 doubles, the most hits in a single season since 1887, when the league played a 154-game season. The numbers remained impressive even when calculated under modern parameters. And yet, who remembers? What went wrong? Why hasn’t he received the fame of a Ruth or Cobb? One reason is that he played in a small market (St. Louis on the Mississippi, where the Cardinals were far more popular) instead of New York or Boston. Another reason is that the 1918 and 1919 seasons were abbreviated by World War I, so his statistics are a bit obscured. In 1920 — his monumental season — he stole 42 bases, which was second in the league and certainly not bad for a first baseman, although he was also a competent pitcher. He was the first baseman for the St. Louis Browns (later to become the Baltimore Orioles), and at the time, first basemen weren’t expected to steal bases! And the Browns were a woeful team, especially by comparison to the Yankees, so his talent was less on display. In fact, Browns fans often referred to their team as “The Terrible Browns.” Sisler hit for a high average, had great power, was an excellent fielder, and stole bases — what more could a player need? It’s a shame he’s not better remembered. Perhaps even more incredible: in 1922, Sisler batted .420 but that batting average wasn’t enough to win the batting title! While he had one of the greatest offensive seasons in baseball history in 1920, a mysterious case of sinusitis ended his 1923, 1924 and 1925 seasons, which effectively ended his chances to be known to modern fans beyond the scope of his early dominance. At the time, sinusitis was a condition for which there was no remedy, and the resulting double vision from a sinus headache effectively ended his career. Sisler returned to the Browns in 1926, but he lost his power, could no longer run and hit only .290; at age 33, his time was over. After his playing career, Sisler managed the Browns from 1924 to 1926, and he was a scout. It isn’t right or fair that he remains a relatively minor name, despite having statistics that are arguably better than those of the more famous players of his time. As they say, better late than never, but this poem hopes to honor a vastly undervalued and often forgotten player, George Sisler. Do you think Jake Paul will be remembered as a legitimate boxer in the future? Whether Jake Paul is destined for boxing immortality is a question even Nostradamus would be hard-pressed to answer with any certainty. Yet, one suspects he'll be remembered, if not as a titan of the ring then certainly as a phenomenon that, for a time, captured the public's collective attention. He embodies the brash confidence, the self-promotion, and the willingness to court controversy that defines the modern age of celebrity. His impact, however, will likely dwindle, fading from the annals of boxing history like a poorly thrown jab. He may be relegated to a footnote, a curiosity, or an asterisk. Perhaps his legacy will be more akin to that of a sideshow barker who, for a fleeting moment, commanded the center ring. His name will likely trigger nostalgic memories, reminding us of the era when celebrity culture and combat sports had a very tumultuous, fascinating, and often ludicrous dance. Will history recall him as a legitimate boxer? The jury may be out for at least a few centuries.

Have dragons or sea serpents ever been seen in the world? If so, why haven't they been captured? Dragons and sea serpents, those mythic leviathans of lore, have long held sway over the human imagination, lurking in the dark unfathomed depths and the fiery heights of legend. Have they, in fact, ever graced the world with their presence, or are they merely the figments of fevered dreams and the exaggerations of yarn-spinning mariners? The accounts of these creatures are as numerous as they are varied, often interwoven with local customs and beliefs, hinting at the occasional, unexplainable sighting. Sailors speak of iridescent, serpentine forms writhing beneath the waves, while others describe colossal, winged beasts, their scales shimmering like a thousand sunsets, soaring above craggy mountain peaks. The fact that none have been brought forth as conclusive proof presents a perplexing paradox demanding some consideration. If such behemoths existed, why have none been snared, subdued, photographed, or otherwise preserved to corroborate their existence? Is this because they dwell, unseen, in unexplored regions and deep-sea chasms, or are their reported appearances mere fleeting illusions? Could it be that they possess an uncanny ability to vanish when discovered, eluding capture through intelligence and a mastery of their domain? If these grand, formidable beings are merely constructs born of the human mind, then why do they persist across countless cultures and time periods? Or, is it because some small bit of truth still manages to ignite the flame of possibility? Regardless, in the absence of tangible evidence, the mystery of dragons and sea serpents continues to entice, enchant, and taunt the realms of both science and storytelling.

What's the name of your church, and what attracts you in there? "The Church of the Open Door" is what we call it, a simple name for a place where anyone can find solace. It's not the gilded extravagance of some cathedrals, nor the hushed austerity of others; it's an embrace, a haven built on the principles of unwavering acceptance and boundless compassion. What draws me? It's the genuine connection, the feeling of belonging, the sanctuary from the harsh realities of a world often consumed by judgment and division. It's the shared belief in the inherent goodness of humanity, and the commitment to nurturing that goodness in ourselves and others. The music, too — a blend of ancient hymns, soulful gospel, and contemporary melodies — elevates the spirit, and the simple act of sharing a meal, a word, or a silent moment of reflection fosters a sense of unity that nourishes the soul.

What relationship do you have with Satan? I’d sooner consort with a viper. Or maybe a gaggle of angry geese. The “Prince of Darkness” and I, well, let's just say our paths rarely cross. How was Mike Tyson generally ranked "all-time" between 1988 and 1991? Was there already a perception that Mike Tyson might be a top 5 heavyweight ever between those years (and between ages 21 and 24)? MIKE TYSON’S RANKING IN THE LATE 1980S AND EARLY 1990S by Michael R. Burch Mike Tyson, unquestionably one of boxing's most dominant forces, would be ranked, not just among the greatest heavyweights of all time, but near the very top. Between 1988 and 1991, at his peak, a consensus had quickly formed, with many considering him a top-5 heavyweight ever. His ferocity in the ring, the speed of his hands, and his knockout power were simply devastating. In 1988, he was undeniably the most feared fighter in the world, in his early twenties. The perception of Tyson as an all-time great was solidified by his string of devastating knockouts, early in his career, and his undisputed title reign. Moreover, his aura was built on an unshakeable image of invincibility. He possessed an undeniable magnetism and, during those years, he was often considered the most exciting athlete in the world, regardless of sport. He was frequently compared to boxing legends like Muhammad Ali, Joe Louis, and Jack Johnson, often with his name on every list. His losses to Buster Douglas, Evander Holyfield, and Lennox Lewis eventually would tarnish his legacy. However, considering his raw skills, devastating power, and the fear that he inflicted upon his opponents during his peak, Tyson's place among the all-time greats was, without a doubt, entrenched. He captured the imagination of the public, crossing over from sports to a larger celebrity status than perhaps any other fighter of the era, with the obvious exception of Ali. His aggressive and often intimidating demeanor was both a blessing and a curse: he was a formidable champion, but his reputation for violence and controversy would follow him throughout his career and would, in the end, derail it.

If Jews don't believe in Jesus, then why make the whole first half of the Bible about them? If the Bible's first half, the Old Testament, chronicles the history, laws, and prophets of the Jewish people, then why would some Christians continue to use it to push forward a Jesus-centered narrative? It's a historical mishmash, a theological jumble, a narrative twist that never feels wholly organic. Consider this: if we’re led to accept the Old Testament, we must accept the history upon which it's based, as well as their traditions, prophecies, and covenants. Yet, after accepting the Old Testament, we’re then told we must also accept that all of it points to a Jesus who ultimately invalidates the covenant itself, if one takes the New Testament literally! How can one whole-heartedly accept texts that Christians claim prefigure Jesus, and still not recognize the inherent conflict? Why, then, should Jews be compelled to worship a figure the texts they revere never foretold as the Messiah? It seems like a way to re-write history, distort texts, and ultimately, colonize their faith with an alien savior.

What star player of the Negro League is thought to be able to challenge the major league but didn't? The immortal Satchel Paige, a pitcher of such extraordinary skill that it seemed almost blasphemous to compare him to mere mortals. Though his career in the Major Leagues finally commenced when he was a seasoned forty-two, the legend of his prowess, a symphony of speed, control, and unparalleled charisma, resonated across the baseball landscape long before his belated arrival. While his actual statistics in the white leagues are but a fragment of his broader achievements, his reputation, cemented by a lifetime of dominance, elevated him to a level of reverence rarely accorded to any athlete, regardless of color, background, or era. He remains the quintessential embodiment, the patron saint, of what might have been.

How was God born? The question is, what a question! A metaphysical conundrum that has troubled theologians and philosophers for epochs. The answer, of course, is that God was not "born," at least not in the conventional sense. Birth implies a beginning, a point in time at which existence commences. But the very essence of God, as conceived by many, is eternal — without a beginning and without an end. God, in this view, has always been and always will be. He is the uncaused cause, the unmoved mover. To ask how God was born is akin to asking what is north of the North Pole: a question that presupposes a framework that doesn’t apply. If you accept God’s existence, then you must reckon with God's timelessness, the negation of a genesis that would necessitate a "before" that could not have possibly occurred. To pose the question of God's birth presupposes a temporal context that diminishes the divine character. If God is infinite, then how can he have a beginning? He cannot.

What are some lesser-known facts or misconceptions about Nimrod? Is there evidence to suggest that he was a historical figure rather than a mythological one? NIMROD: MYTH, LEGEND OR FACT? by Michael R. Burch There are a number of lesser-known facts about Nimrod, and a number of misconceptions, too. For example, Nimrod is sometimes described in an overly-simplistic fashion as either a wicked villain or a heroic king, but in reality, he was likely a bit of both. The term "Nimrod" is often used as a synonym for a great hunter, deriving from the biblical account of Nimrod as "a mighty hunter before the Lord" (Genesis 10:9). This is the most popular misconception. People often equate his hunting prowess with a kind of nobility. This may be true, but the Bible doesn’t give us the answers to all our questions. Nimrod is presented in the Bible as a descendant of Ham, one of Noah’s sons, and the founder of several ancient cities in Mesopotamia, including Babel (Babylon), Erech (Uruk), Akkad, and Calneh. The biblical account positions Nimrod as a significant figure in early post-Flood civilizations. Another less-known fact is that Nimrod's name, in the Hebrew language, likely means "we shall rebel" or "let us rebel." This etymological analysis gives a clue to Nimrod’s actual intent when he constructed the Tower of Babel, which appears to have been to usurp control of heaven. The Tower of Babel is often misunderstood, too, as an attempt at a physical structure that would allow humanity to ascend to the heavens and reach God; it was that. But it was also, more crucially, a brazen challenge to the divine authority, a rebellion against God’s sovereignty and a blatant attempt to establish humanity’s control over the cosmos. Because of this, I believe that Nimrod was a real figure. There is actually considerable evidence to suggest that Nimrod was a historical figure, rather than a purely mythological one. Archaeological findings in Mesopotamia, specifically in areas linked to Nimrod and the cities he founded, support the existence of powerful rulers and advanced civilizations during the time frame attributed to Nimrod in the Bible. The fact that Nimrod is referenced in multiple ancient texts and traditions lends credibility to his historical existence. Many scholars see Nimrod as a powerful king who helped with the actual construction of the Tower of Babel. But this is speculative, and it may never be known for sure. However, the fact that Nimrod appears in multiple ancient texts suggests that he was, or was believed to have been, a real person.

Why don't people believe in God? What if I told you that there is a God and that I saw the Lord’s spirits with my own eyes? My experiences might be dismissed as hallucinations, but my soul assures me, to be so utterly dismissive, with no desire to understand, is merely the arrogance of the unbeliever. What if I told you that God is far more complex than the Bible's simplified depictions would suggest? What if I described a sublime being whose essence is reflected in the beauty of the Milky Way, the unfathomable depths of the Mariana Trench, and the astonishing complexity of the human brain? What if I told you this God is love and the universe is His canvas? What if the doubters' lack of belief stems from a pre-imposed conclusion based on limited information? What if that were the case? This God has no use for self-worship, and if you can grasp that, you will begin to see. What could he want with temples, chants, and the adulation of the masses? Nothing at all.

When did the U.S. first claim victory over the Third Reich? The U.S. never officially declared victory over the Third Reich, as such. The Allies, including the United States, accepted Germany's unconditional surrender on May 8, 1945, known as Victory in Europe Day (V-E Day), effectively ending the war in Europe. However, the U.S. did not make a separate, formal declaration because the Allied forces acted in concert to crush the Nazi regime. After Japan surrendered, the U.S. did declare victory in the Pacific Theater of the war and, by extension, in World War II. The U.S. victory was a collective effort with its allies.

Why did the Israelites kill all the people in the city of Ai in Joshua 8:24-30? I’m struggling to understand why God would instruct them to do something like this. I find it difficult to accept the premise that the Lord, in all His supposed benevolence, would ever order the savage slaughter of an entire town, including women, children, and animals, solely based on the dubious claims of some desert tribe. It clashes so blatantly with any reasonable measure of ethics or decency. Such actions, as recounted in the Old Testament, are more befitting a bloodthirsty warlord than a deity. I reject the assertion that these events were divinely ordained. I question the motives and actions of the authors of the tale, and I consider the implications of such stories unsettling to anyone of good conscience. If these are the acts of a god, then I cannot fathom how anyone would want to worship him.

Who is considered the most powerful mythical being, despite there being no evidence of its existence? The most powerful mythical being? That, of course, depends on who you ask and when you ask them! But let’s disregard the obvious, like the Big Guy Upstairs—Yahweh, Jehovah—who, as I’ve pointed out before, seems more of a celestial terrorist than a benevolent protector. Let’s talk about characters who possess power, even if they are not real: the ones who could level Olympus, if they had to; the ones who could incinerate galaxies, if they wanted to; the ones who made the others tremble in their sandals. For me, that would have to be the Titans, and particularly, the most powerful Titan of all—Kronos, sometimes spelled Cronus. As it says in Hesiod’s *Theogony*, Kronos was a god of tremendous cunning and guile and, indeed, one of the original Titans, offspring of Gaia and Uranus. And he was fearsome. He castrated his father, Uranus, after being encouraged to do so by his mother, Gaia and his siblings. Then Kronos swallowed each of his children immediately after they were born. That’s right: he ate his own children! His wife, Rhea, managed to save one—Zeus—who overthrew his father, and forced him to vomit up his siblings, but can there be any doubt about the power of a god who could do such barbaric, horrific things? Zeus was pretty powerful, sure, but he was only powerful because he outsmarted his dad, and was able to lead an uprising of his siblings. And that, dear friends, is power. Who’s the most powerful mythical being? For me, it will always be Kronos, the Titan who literally devoured his own progeny.

If God created life then who created God? Religion insist God created everything but whenever you ask where did God come from they go silent. If you have nothing then how can you create something? The cosmos is a vast and intricate tapestry, a symphony of existence that hums with questions that resonate across millennia. If a divine being conjured it all, the grand stage, the players, the script, then where does the agency originate? The conundrum of origins. The void before the beginning. The inescapable, maddening paradox. If nothing precedes God, then is He not as much a product of the void as we? We find them mute, clutching their dogma like totems. The very substance of deity—a conceptual edifice—is a breathtaking feat of creation, the very essence they attribute to their celestial architect. A cosmic architect must have needed a craftsman, or were they both spawned from a vacuum? And if this primordial being, the progenitor of all, exists independent of the universe as we know it, why does such power exhibit any weakness? If He is all, why does anything exist outside of it?

Why do some people still don’t believe Jesus was resurrected when they proved it with the Shroud of Turin? The Shroud of Turin, the “proof," is itself as fanciful as a unicorn, or the notion that Christ was resurrected. One need only glance at the image, with its impossible anatomy, to see that a deception is afoot. The figure’s arms extend like those of a scarecrow; its hands are clearly misshapen. Not even the most fervent believer seems able to reconcile these obvious flaws with reality. If the Shroud were a true relic of the resurrection, wouldn’t God provide something more, well, believable? The answer, of course, is that He would because there is no evidence—the Resurrection myth is just that—a myth constructed in the fevered imaginations of long-dead storytellers. It's as simple as that. And those who would cling fast to this particular piece of flotsam are grasping at straws.

Why is Wilt Chamberlain not considered the greatest player of all time when his numbers are better than everybody's except Michael Jordan and Lebron James? Wilt Chamberlain’s stats were, indeed, phenomenal—arguably unmatched. His scoring records alone are staggering, yet debate rages about his place among basketball's pantheon. Several well-grounded counterarguments have steadily chipped away at his claim to the G.O.A.T. throne. First, the era of the “Big Dipper” was vastly different. The league was smaller and less talented, with a slower pace, fewer teams, and less emphasis on defense. Second, Chamberlain played on teams that, despite his dominance, didn’t win as much as one might expect. His championship resume is good but not superlative. The narrative is simple: incredible numbers, but some shortcomings. His career presents a fascinating paradox, challenging basketball fans to weigh individual stats against team success and the evolution of the game. Still, his sheer dominance cannot to be ignored. The debate, though, is likely to continue.

Which inaccuracies written about a famous historical figure have not been successfully corrected and for what particular reasons? The most prevalent, egregious and tenacious misrepresentation of a famous figure, I would argue, concerns the life and death of Julius Caesar. For centuries, Shakespeare’s portrayal has lingered in the collective consciousness, casting Caesar as a noble, stoic leader betrayed by a cadre of envious assassins. That depiction of the leader, and not the conspirators, as a tragic hero remains firmly planted, despite a wealth of historical evidence — painstakingly amassed over centuries — to the contrary. The primary culprits for this enduring myth are, of course, literary devices: For dramatic purposes, Shakespeare had to frame Caesar’s assassination as a betrayal, a result of a once-great man succumbing to hubris. This is far more dramatically compelling than the historical truth, which is that Caesar was a ruthless tyrant, who effectively ended the Roman Republic, making himself dictator for life and initiating the decline of Rome. The reasons for this widespread misrepresentation are legion. It is often more palatable to celebrate a fallen leader — particularly one seen from afar -- than to confront the moral complexities of true life. Furthermore, popular culture naturally favors captivating narratives, and the image of a noble leader felled by betrayers offers a more romanticized story than the far more likely reality. Finally, it’s easier to simply accept the popularized accounts which conveniently gloss over the less savory aspects of Caesar’s relentless ambition and tyrannical governance, allowing the image to persist.

Why don't you realise that most people go to hell? Most of the earth’s inhabitants—and that includes the vast majority of those who’ve ever lived—are damned, because of their alleged sins. Why would a supposedly loving God consign billions of individuals to eternal torment, or even, as some faith-based institutions insist, “temporary” torment? If those with faith wish to assert that God is loving and merciful, they’ll have to explain the horrific, unrelenting horrors facing children in wars fought over God, and for God’s sake. To be clear: as a rational, reasonable human being, I will never accept that a God who loves all of us, as advertised, would then inflict such wretched punishments and endless suffering. If there is a God, and I begin to believe, I’ll need him to prove it, and until he can convince me otherwise, I'll respectfully decline.

What do the symbols in William Blake's "The Tyger" represent? William Blake's "The Tyger" pulses with the vibrant symbology of the Romantic era, echoing the very spirit of the sublime. The Tyger, with its ferocious beauty, embodies the untamed potential of the human imagination, reflecting both the creative and destructive forces inherent in the Divine. Consider the blacksmith's furnace, from which the Tyger is forged. This imagery suggests creation through intense heat and pressure, mirroring the fiery passions that shape human nature. The "forests of the night" into which the Tyger prowls symbolize the dark recesses of the unconscious mind, where primal instincts and profound mysteries reside. The tiger is the embodiment of power, a creature of incredible strength and beauty, but also a predator, suggesting the duality of good and evil, beauty and terror, the creator and the destroyer. The Lamb of the companion poem, “The Lamb,” represents gentleness, innocence, and the divine love of God. The poem, through its contrasting images, challenges the reader to reconcile the presence of both benevolent and wrathful forces in the universe, and the role of the creator in the existence of both. The poem's haunting questions, and the implicit suggestion that the same creator fashioned both the lamb and the tiger, underscores this enigmatic duality, leaving us to ponder the complex nature of existence and the source of both beauty and terror in the world. The poem’s success—of course—derives from leaving the reader, the audience, to grapple with these complex questions.

What is the origin of King Arthur? Is he a historical figure or a fictional character created from various historical figures? The Arthurian tales, as they exist today, are a tapestry woven from threads of history, myth, folklore, and, I suspect, a healthy dose of wishful thinking. Pinpointing a single, definitive "King Arthur" is like trying to seize smoke. The most compelling evidence leans toward a real, albeit shadowy, figure who served as a kernel around which the legend grew and expanded. The prevailing theory points to a Romano-British war leader from the late 5th or early 6th century, a period marked by the decline of Roman influence and the rise of Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. This historical Arthur, if he existed, likely fought against the invading Saxons, perhaps leading Britons to victory in pivotal battles. His name, or something similar, might have been a title used in defense of Britain from various conquerors. Over time, his exploits, embellished by bards, poets, and storytellers, morphed into the Arthur we now know—a king of unparalleled valor, surrounded by knights, magic and chivalry, reigning over the utopian kingdom of Camelot. These embellishments drew upon Celtic myths, Christian traditions, and the romantic literary conventions. Whether Arthur was a historical man or merely a synthesis of multiple warriors, the stories took on a life of their own, evolving through centuries, from the Welsh *Mabinogion* to the works of Geoffrey of Monmouth (the chief architect of Arthurian legend), Chrétien de Troyes, and Sir Thomas Malory. These tales are a cultural phenomenon and are a testament to the human yearning for heroism, idealized governance, and a world where courage, honor, and loyalty prevail. The search for the "real" Arthur continues to fascinate—a quest for the truth that lies beneath the gilded surface of legend. It’s much like gazing at the stars: what we see is the light from an age long past, but the source itself may be hidden from sight.

What are some of the most bizarre Bible verses in the Old Testament? What is the most bizarre thing you’ve ever seen? The answer is almost certainly not in the Bible. As a former evangelical, I know the Bible, and I can tell you it’s full of bizarre verses. But what is bizarre to us, the 21st century, is often a routine for those who lived at the time. Consider these verses, among many others: 1.) Deuteronomy 25:11–12: “When men strive together one with another, and the wife of the one draweth near for to deliver her husband out of the hand of him that smiteth him, and putteth forth her hand, and taketh him by the secret parts: Then thou shalt cut off her hand, thine eye shall not pity her.” 2.) Isaiah 13:16: “Their children also shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes; their houses shall be spoiled and their wives ravished.” 3.) II Kings 2:23-24: “And he went up from thence unto Bethel: and as he was going up by the way, there came forth little children out of the city, and mocked him, and said unto him, Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head. And he turned back, and looked on them, and cursed them in the name of the Lord. And there came forth two she bears out of the wood, and tare forty and two children of them.” 4.) Judges 3:21: “And Ehud reached with his left hand, and took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into the belly.” 5.) Genesis 19:8: “Behold now, I have two daughters which have not known man; let me, I pray you, bring them out unto you, and do ye to them as is good in your eyes: only unto these men do nothing; for therefore came they under the shadow of my roof.” Why are these verses so bizarre to us? Because they involve extreme violence, including child murder; sexual assault; and misogyny. But the ancient authors, writing in a time when life was cheap, believed that these were acts for a god that was just. How would you feel if every day, you woke up and had to worry about a bear mauling your children to death?

Is there a historical figure who is widely known but whose life remains a mystery? The identity of William Shakespeare, arguably the world’s most famous writer, remains perhaps the greatest historical literary mystery. We know snippets about his life as well as his business dealings, including his roles as an actor, a playwright, and a shareholder in a playing company. However, nearly everything known about Shakespeare can be summed up in about 100 pages — and this includes his will and the historical records of his life in Stratford-upon-Avon. The Bard’s actual personal life, including his relationships, his religious beliefs, and the influences that shaped his works, remain a matter of speculation and debate. The enduring questions — what exactly did Shakespeare look like, how did he write so many plays of such vast scope and complexity, and to whom did he dedicate so many intimate sonnets — remain largely unanswered. His origins, aside from his documented birth and death, are frustratingly cloaked in obscurity. A major problem in any discussion or investigation of “Shakespeare’s Life” is how little material there is to analyze. There’s no complete biography, no diary, few surviving letters, and the handful of details we do have consist largely of local legal and financial transactions. In short, almost all the known details relate to his business. What remains are the voluminous works of Shakespeare, but it is these very works that have spurred theories and arguments about the man and his life since the seventeenth century. This dearth of evidence has led to the Shakespeare authorship question, as multiple figures have been nominated to be the true author of Shakespeare’s plays, including Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe, and the Earl of Oxford; the Shakespeare authorship question continues to vex scholars to this day.

Why would people blame God for abuse, famine, psychopath murders or similar when those are choices an actions of men/women? If humans are free to make their own choices whether good or evil, why blame God? I am constantly amazed at the ease some people have in blaming God for every evil act man perpetrates, while conveniently omitting those events which are good. If a hurricane levels an orphanage, God is to blame. If a child is saved from a burning building, well, that’s just luck. It's baffling to witness the willful blindness of those who select only the bad and lay them solely on God’s shoulders, conveniently sidelining human agency. Perhaps they find comfort in the certainty of their own victimhood, or perhaps it’s simply easier to dismiss as supernatural forces instead of facing the harsh realities of humanity’s failings. It is a curious paradox.

Exactly when did Christians start believing in a triune God - "one God in three persons"? Did the apostles and writers of the New Testament believe in "one God in three persons"? Is this what Jesus taught? The earliest Christians, those who lived closest in time to Jesus and his apostles, did not have a fully developed understanding of the Trinity. While the concept of God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, is present in the New Testament, the idea of a single divine essence shared by three distinct persons was a product of later theological reflection. The apostles certainly believed in God as a singular entity, with Jesus as the Son of God, and the presence of the Holy Spirit active among them. However, the precise nature of their relationship within that singular Godhead was not definitively articulated. Jesus himself did not explicitly teach the doctrine of the Trinity in the way it would later be systematized. Instead, he spoke of his own relationship with God the Father in terms of obedience and unique sonship, along with the promise of the Holy Spirit in the future. It took centuries of debate, including heretical challenges and complex theological arguments, for the doctrine of the Trinity to take shape, and eventually be formalized in the Nicene Creed, a document summarizing the essential beliefs of the Christian faith. It was a process of interpretation and refinement, seeking to express the complex interplay of divine figures in a coherent, unified declaration of faith.

Does the voice of God sound like thunder, or is the voice quiet? The voice of God, if a voice there be, likely sounds like a sigh, perhaps a whisper, or a rustling of leaves when the wind stirs the branches. Maybe it's the feeling of a gentle touch upon your cheek or a deep feeling of awe as you gaze upon the night sky. It could be a feeling, rather than a sound, a sense of purpose, a sudden understanding, an inkling of connectedness. Or, perhaps, the voice of God is silence, the absence of sound itself, the space in which all other things exist. Whether it booms like thunder or murmurs like a prayer, it depends on each heart and soul. Yet, regardless of the sound, the message, if there is any, must be one of love and peace. For how could a creator filled with hate bring forth a world of beauty?

Which books of the Bible have been proven to be forgeries by modern scholars? Which books of the Bible have been proven to be written by other than the claimed authors by modern scholars? The answer, of course, is "all of them," or close enough. The overwhelming majority of biblical scholars will tell you that the Bible’s authorship is largely unknown. Most of the Old and New Testaments were compiled long after the supposed events, and even by the time the texts were being “canonized”—that is, selected for their inclusion in the Bible—the original authors of the Gospels, for example, were unknown. Some books may have been written by the authors’ claimed namesakes, but there is no proof, only conjecture. But let’s look more closely at the details that the scholarly consensus would admit: The Gospels, for example, written centuries after the putative events. The books of James, Peter, and John, their authorship debated, with the majority of scholarly consensus pointing to other writers. The letters ascribed to Paul, some of which are considered to be authentic and others not, as these were compiled over decades. And while there is the Book of Mormon and other texts claiming divine origin, they've all been challenged and rejected. As for which biblical books, in particular, have been proven to be forgeries based on the most meticulous research, the answer is all of them. The books of Baruch, Tobit, Judith, and many other Old testament books were excluded by most churches.

Have there been any baseball players who had a great start but ended up having a terrible career? Yes, there have been several baseball players who burst onto the scene with sensational debuts, only to fade into obscurity or underperform significantly later in their careers. These "one-hit wonders," or more accurately, one-season wonders, often tantalize fans with glimpses of extraordinary talent, but a myriad of factors can contribute to their inability to sustain that initial success. Injuries, both physical and mental, a failure to adapt to the league's ever-evolving strategies, and the pressures of heightened expectations can all play a role in derailing promising careers. Oftentimes, as the league adjusts to a player’s strengths, weaknesses begin to manifest. The ability to adapt to a change is necessary and if lacking, a player may quickly find themselves at the edge of a roster. Another factor is the sudden influx of wealth, fans and media. This "pressure cooker" environment can be damaging to a player who is unprepared for the responsibility. Some players succumb to the limelight, their careers faltering under the weight of sudden fame. The baseball gods, it seems, are often as fickle as the fans.

Is belief in God justified? It depends, of course, on the god. The ancient Greeks had a pantheon of gods and goddesses, and the Romans cloned the Greeks’ pantheon with different names. Norse mythology and Egyptian mythology also had their gods, and the Aztecs had their own bloodthirsty gods. Every culture has had gods, including Christians, Jews, and Muslims, but they all worship the same god: the horrendous Yahweh. So why do some people believe and others do not? For the theists—those who do believe—the explanations for the existence of their gods are typically faith, religious texts, tradition, personal experiences, and appeals to the “origin” of creation. For the atheists—those who do not believe—the explanations are typically arguments against the existence of a god or gods because of the apparent absence of evidence, as well as logical, moral, or scientific considerations. The atheists can also make the argument that belief in gods is frequently linked to negative phenomena like intolerance, dogma, violence, fear of death and general ignorance. For me, belief in the Abrahamic god is not justified.

Was Paul ever referred to as a Rabbi? No. The Apostle Paul was never referred to as a Rabbi, a member of the Jewish clergy. Nor was he ever described as a Rabbi by any of the apostles or other leaders of the early Christian church, including James "the brother of Jesus." In fact, there is no evidence in the New Testament to support a claim that Paul was a Rabbi. Instead, Paul claimed to be a Pharisee: "circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee" (Philippians 3:5, King James Version). The other apostles never refer to Paul as a Rabbi, and there is no record of Paul himself using the term to describe himself. In fact, it is highly unlikely that anyone describing themselves as a “servant of God” (Romans 1:1) would simultaneously claim the title of Rabbi, which means “teacher of the Torah.” Paul taught and preached throughout the Roman Empire and beyond. Paul’s teachings emphasized Jesus Christ, his crucifixion and resurrection, and faith in Jesus as the key to salvation. Paul's writings have had an enormous influence on both Christianity and Western civilization. He wrote at least seven, and possibly thirteen, of the books of the New Testament. In the earliest of his letters, Paul consistently calls himself an apostle, not a Rabbi, and refers to himself as Christ's “bond-servant.”

Why didn’t God know what Adam and Eve will do after forbidding them from doing wrong? God is, in fact, omniscient, the ultimate authority across all. I believe it is a matter of faith, or perhaps belief in free will. As free agents, they may choose any path. Then why would God set them up just to let them fall? That is the ultimate conundrum that has plagued me for decades now. Why, precisely, did God forbid the fruit? Would his creation have remained pure if he hadn't erected an obstacle—one his "children" were destined to fail to surmount? And then again, the Devil, who knows where he came from. All this talk of "temptation." Who put the temptation there? And if that ancient Serpent, or whatever form the Devil took, was indeed so all-powerful and so malevolent, what kind of "game" are we all engaged in? I suppose the Bible has one explanation, but I'm not sold that it's the only one.

Why is the Christian God so insecure that he needs worship? The "loving" Christian God, Yahweh, also has a penchant for demanding total obedience—or else. His behavior often seems petulant rather than paternal, a far cry from the benevolent deity often portrayed in stained-glass windows. For a being allegedly omnipotent, omniscient, and omnipresent, it is a curious quirk that he needs constant reassurance from humankind. The notion that an all-powerful creator would require the fervent adoration of his creations is, to put it mildly, peculiar. One might anticipate divine indifference, not a deity with what appears, at times, to be a fragile ego. This insecurity, if it can be labeled such, is not only baffling but also the cornerstone of centuries of religious dogma and, alas, many bloody conflicts. If Yahweh truly possessed the qualities attributed to him, the need for constant praise would be entirely absent, rendering the whole concept of religious devotion seemingly superfluous.

What are some results since you walked away from God? I’ve found the world remains exactly what it was before: a whirling sphere hurtling through the void. The sun still shines, the rain still falls, and the flowers still sprout forth in spring, as ever before. The greedy, the foolish, and the cruel continue to dominate, as always happened. I feel no more enlightened. No less foolish. No more loved. No more hated. There are moments of exquisite joy and others of abject despair. They have nothing to do with the existence or nonexistence of any deus ex machina. The same trials present themselves, over and over, as they always have. As for what’s changed? Before, I was a man tormented by the fear of an eternity of torment. That fear is gone. Now, I am simply a man hoping for a few more moments of joy. So I suppose what has changed is everything. And nothing.

Who are the most powerful gods, in order? Power is an elusive concept, ever shifting and subject to the vagaries of faith, circumstance, and perception. Thus, ranking the most powerful gods is a fool's errand, yet a perpetually engaging one. To even begin, we must define power. Does it mean dominion over realms, the ability to influence mortal affairs, or the sheer awe and terror inspired by a god's name? For my ranking, I'll consider all these factors, and more, while also paying deference—as I often do—to those who have wielded their influence in poetry, literature, and the arts. The following is entirely subjective. First, Zeus, the king of the gods, both Olympian and, at one point, Mesopotamian, but Zeus always reigns supreme. Then, second, is Odin, the all father, of the ancient Norse pantheon. Third, is the almighty, the great cosmic everything, Yahweh, who at minimum is highly influential. Forth, is Ra, the ancient Egyptian sun god. And fifth, is the Greek goddess, mighty Hera. Sixth is the Roman goddess Juno, who as the Roman counterpart of Hera, often gets overlooked – until she sends her wrath! Seventh is the mighty Hindu god, Shiva. Eighth, is the goddess of love, Aphrodite. Ninth is the Celtic god Cernunnos, who, despite his limited purview, has shown remarkable persistence, and a great connection to the natural world. Tenth, and last, is the Christian god, known better as Jesus, who, in his suffering and sacrifice, has inspired untold millions.

The story of Joseph as the husband of Mary seems somewhat contrived. Since Jesus is referred to in one of the Gospels as the son of Mary (not the son of Joseph), is it possible that Jesus was illegitimate? In the Gospel accounts, Joseph is presented and described as a carpenter. But beyond his trade, Joseph is a man of profound inner stillness, and the Bible tells us that he was a “just man.” Thus, Joseph was given the singular honor of being the one who adopted Jesus as his legal son, and that is no small honor. The virgin birth, and the associated supernatural aspects of the Annunciation, appear to contradict Joseph's very nature and that of his betrothed. Yet he obeyed the command of an angel and became the earthly parent of Jesus. Might Joseph have struggled with the knowledge that he was not the father of his betrothed’s child? It is very difficult to say. But if one is to believe the Gospel accounts, Joseph would have trusted in the divine will. Was there an element of faith, or perhaps desperation, in Joseph’s decision to marry Mary and protect her son? If there were, it may be only human to wonder what that element would be.

If you could spend a day with any historical figure, who would it be and what would you do? If given the chance, I would journey back to the court of the Florentine Medici and spend a day with Leonardo da Vinci. We would not speak of his Mona Lisa, the sublime beauty of which speaks for itself; nor would we delve into the scientific enigmas that captivated his formidable intellect. No, our day would be spent in his workshop, surrounded by the tools of his trade, observing the genesis of his creations. I would watch him sketch in his notebooks, the restless energy of his hand capturing the essence of form and motion, shaping light and shadow with the swift, decisive strokes of a master. We would pore over the complex mechanisms of his inventions, discussing the interplay of art, science, and the sheer joy of creation. Perhaps, if the day were propitious, we could even collaborate on a project, melding his genius with my own humble attempts. And in the evening, as the Tuscan sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows across the Arno, we would share a simple meal, and I would listen intently, absorbing the wisdom of a man for whom the world was an endless canvas, a source of infinite wonder and discovery, a challenge to be met with unrelenting curiosity and boundless creativity.

Is believing in a God reasonable? Or is belief in a deity simply faith, hope, perhaps even desperation? I recently debated a friend, and he suggested — with as much patience as he could muster — that I might want to give God a chance. This is what I have gathered from my interactions with many believers over the years: It is not simply that they “believe,” but that they “know." And yet I continue to have faith (or perhaps not faith) in the scientific method, and the rationalist’s creed. So the debate continues in my mind, and from a distance, I can look back on years in which I earnestly “sought God,” always without the hoped-for result. "Is believing in a God reasonable?" isn’t a question with an easy answer.

Is God imaginary? I’ve met so many people who believe in various Gods and Goddesses that I can’t possibly doubt that belief is a powerful and real phenomenon. Whether the objects of such faith are actual or imaginary is, in my humble opinion, a matter of conjecture. But I do not see any reason to be convinced of the existence of *any* God, including all of the ones invented by humankind. I have found no proof that there are any gods or goddesses beyond the ones we create for ourselves. Indeed, the very concept of “God” is problematic. It is often used to describe a being or force that is beyond human understanding, yet the specific attributes of these divine entities vary wildly across cultures and religions. Such contradictions lead me to believe in very little outside of the physical world. And if you ask me to believe in *a* God, I would ask you to provide a plausible explanation of why the other thousands of gods and goddesses, all believed in with sincerity by others, are fake. And explain why the one you worship is the one *true* God? If you cannot offer an explanation, then I will not agree.

What is the conversation between Moses and Elijah at Mount Tabor as described in the Bible by Luke and Mark? WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT MOSES, ELIJAH AND JESUS AT MOUNT TABOR BY MICHAEL R. BURCH Luke 9:28-36 Mark 9:2-8 The brief passage in Luke, as well as Mark, says that Moses and Elijah appeared "in glory" and spoke with Jesus. That's it. The Gospel does not tell us what Moses and Elijah said to Jesus. The text does not describe what exactly they looked like, apart from their manifestation "in glory." So we have no way of knowing what was actually discussed at Mount Tabor. We do, however, know the participants. Moses, the founder and lawgiver of Israel. Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, and it was Moses to whom God spoke on Mount Sinai. Elijah was a prophet who lived centuries after Moses and challenged the worship of the false god Baal. Elijah is the prophet of fire, who performed miracles and challenged the corrupt priests of Baal. Jesus, the central figure of Christianity. The Bible describes Jesus as the son of God who came to Earth to save humanity, and he supposedly spoke to Moses and Elijah. The context of the event, the Transfiguration, is noteworthy. Jesus took three of his closest disciples—Peter, John, and James—to a high mountain, where he was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and his clothes became dazzling white. This event is significant because it affirms Jesus's divinity and his place in God’s plan, and, in one of the Bible's rare instances, we may see something of what can occur after a spirit sheds its mortal coil. It is, in essence, the afterlife's great unveiling. As the text states, Moses and Elijah “appeared” in glory, speaking with Jesus. Then the disciples saw the glory of God in the form of a bright cloud, and a voice came from the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, whom I have chosen; listen to him.” The appearance of Moses and Elijah can be understood as an affirmation that Jesus is the fulfillment of the Law (Moses) and the Prophets (Elijah). Many theological interpretations state that the presence of Moses and Elijah symbolizes that to Jesus, the Law and Prophecy both bear witness. Both are present at the Transfiguration. The Gospels’ accounts suggest an immense significance to the event. For many Christians, the Transfiguration is a moment when Jesus's identity as the Son of God is revealed to his disciples, not some casual conversation.

Which poem is more iconic, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland's Jabberwocky or The Jungle Book's The Law of the Jungle? Frankly, this is a devilishly difficult question, a veritable Rubik’s Cube of literary significance. Both wield an undeniable resonance, etched into the collective consciousness like ancient runes. “Jabberwocky,” with its nonsensical brilliance, its portmanteau artistry, and its utter disregard for the mundane, remains a cornerstone of linguistic play. It’s a poem that dances on the edge of meaning, beckoning us into a world where language itself is malleable clay, a whimsical tapestry woven from the threads of pure invention. But “The Law of the Jungle,” with its stark pronouncements and Kipling’s enduring storytelling power, remains ever relevant. It’s a code of conduct, a set of rules for survival, a cautionary tale in the grand scheme of things. It speaks not of unicorns and the impossible but of how to live and thrive. It is a lesson in the brutal beauty of existence. If pressed, I suppose one could argue that "Jabberwocky" is more universally recognized, but "The Law of the Jungle" is the more enduring because it speaks to a very real aspect of existence. Perhaps the question itself is a false dichotomy. Both poems— and tales— stand on two separate, if closely aligned, pillars. But if I were forced to choose a single, more iconic poem, I might choose one that contains a line that you already know, a bit of verse to make you look at the world with new eyes: This poem is a masterpiece of linguistic creativity and its lines "Beware the Jabberwock, my son! The jaws that bite, the claws that catch!" have endured the tests of time, or have they?

Why are there so many people who pick Michael Jordan and other, newer players as the basketball GOAT over Wilt Chamberlain? The numbers don’t lie. Wilt Chamberlain did things in basketball that no one else has ever done, and no one else ever will. His scoring records alone seem almost to belong to another sport. But it’s a matter of perception. The perception of Chamberlain is that he was a selfish, statistics-obsessed player who often failed to lead his teams to victory. He’s like the strong, silent, overachieving kid you knew in high school who always seemed to lack some essential element of “cool.” Then along came Michael Jordan, whose entire career was the stuff of legends. He was the clutch player, the winner who dominated his competition and always, always finished the job. And his charisma? Unmatchable. Jordan was the perfect confluence of athleticism, grace, skill, and relentless determination. All this, combined with his impeccable marketing, made him more than just a basketball player; he was a global phenomenon, a brand. People are drawn to the narrative. Jordan’s narrative is one of triumph, and the game’s ultimate triumph is winning the championship. Also, you have to contend with cultural factors. People who grew up watching Jordan are much more likely to view him as the GOAT than those who saw Chamberlain’s prime. Nostalgia and personal experience tend to play a significant part in such debates.

Why in Major League Baseball does a scuffed up baseball make a difference? A scuffed up baseball, though seemingly a minor detail, can significantly impact a game because it alters the aerodynamics and unpredictability of the ball's flight through the air. The scuffs disrupt the smooth surface, creating turbulence and drag in ways that can deceive hitters. A pitcher can exploit these imperfections to induce more movement on their pitches—a fastball that subtly dips, a curveball that breaks more sharply. This can lead to weak contact, swings and misses, and ultimately, a pitcher's dominance over a hitter. For hitters, a scuffed ball is more likely to wobble in flight, making it harder to track. The reduced friction can also affect the carry and distance of the ball, potentially ruining a batter's timing. While some might see a scuff as a simple cosmetic flaw, knowing this, the effect is real, and teams and players frequently lobby for or against them.

Are there any MLB players who are disliked by their teammates? More often than not, baseball players, like others, tend to dislike people who are egocentric, selfish, and unwilling to work with the team. Also, the players who are perpetually late, always making excuses, or frequently exhibit some other form of bad behavior also get under teammates’ skin. However, many other factors that could contribute include: a player’s political or religious beliefs; a player’s association with scandals; a player’s perceived entitlement; a player’s poor work ethic; a player not being a ‘good sport’ when he loses; or the player’s general personality being simply incompatible with that of his other team members. Perhaps the most disliked players, however, tend to be those who make the team worse by underperforming or, even worse, players who are thought to have bad attitudes, especially if those attitudes infect the rest of the team. The players may simply not like a player who is not a good team member or who just doesn't fit in properly. The players usually band together against players whom they see as being a detriment to their shared enterprise.

Can a definitive "greatest of all time" be determined in all sports? Most assuredly not! To an ardent fan, their favorite athlete will always be the GOAT. Ask a casual observer, and they’ll likely roll their eyes. Every sport—nay, even every *era* of every sport—possesses its own unique metrics, skill sets, and levels of competition. The game itself has evolved. Babe Ruth would likely be a solid hitter in modern baseball though not the dominating force he once was, but his pitching…forget about it! Modern pitchers would laugh him off the mound. Is Barry Bonds the best hitter ever? Perhaps. But he cheated; some say, all of them did, and if he's not the GOAT, who is? Same with football. How do you compare Jim Thorpe’s feats to those of Tom Brady? It’s like comparing apples and oranges; they played different games. Even within a single sport, such as the world of boxing, we can argue for hours: Ali, Frazier, Tyson, Leonard, or Armstrong—who was the best? Ultimately, greatness, like beauty, is often in the eye (and heart) of the beholder, no matter what the "experts" have to say.

People who were around in 1974, who did you pick to win Ali vs Foreman? Most of us picked Foreman, hands down. He seemed invincible, a fearsome titan of a man, crushing all before him. Ali was supposed to be washed up, past his prime, a relic of a bygone era. He had already lost to Frazier, and the narrative was that Foreman would obliterate him. There wasn't a lot of love for Ali at that time. He was seen as a loudmouth, a draft dodger, though his star would soon rise again in the court of public opinion. But in Zaire, in the shadow of the jungle, Ali would unleash his "rope-a-dope" strategy, and shock the world. I remember the electric buzz, the disbelief during the fight: “Ali, Boma ye!” he would yell at Foreman. It was the event of the century, and I was glued to the television, stunned. I still remember that feeling of awe, the moment Ali turned the tide. It was one of the most memorable moments in sports history.

According to religious beliefs, did God create all things including Hell, Heaven, and Earth? Many religious faiths maintain, yes, that God is, in fact, the architect of all Creation—the cosmos itself, our planet and its multifarious life, as well as both the ethereal realms of Heaven and the fiery depths of Hell. The very architecture of reality is, in this view, a divine expression, a testament to the Almighty's boundless power.

Which do you believe is true, creationism or evolutionism? I believe scientific consensus is more credible than dogma. As a result, I'm a proponent of evolution, which is a scientifically-supported theory. What is actually "believed" is far in excess of what is true. The "truth," if it exists, is far less complicated than the myriad and mutable beliefs of mankind, most of whom seem to follow a path that leads to a conclusion other than the one stated to be desired. If you “believe” in evolution, how do you explain Adam and Eve and the Garden of Eden? Well first, I don't believe in Adam and Eve, any more than I believe in the gods of Greece or the Norsemen or the Tooth Fairy or the Cookie Monster. Those are all lovely myths, but mythologies are not true. If there was ever an actual Adam and Eve, any evidence is long, long gone--as is the case with the Garden of Eden. Nor is there scientific evidence to support the “truth” of either. There's nothing to confirm such “tales” and much to disprove, especially the literalist interpretation of the Bible that seeks to refute science. The truth is often more mysterious than we suspect, not simply "hidden," but forever and infinitely beyond human capability. I understand that my belief—that the scientific evidence is undeniable in favor of evolution—may not convince you to believe as I do, but it is truth to me.

On The Simpsons, if Homer enjoys hell because he is forced to eat all of the donuts in the world, then what kind of hell would he not like that would be a horrifying experience for him? Homer Simpson wouldn’t like hell if he were forced to engage in actual *work*—even if it was work that involved donuts. Imagine Homer chained to an assembly line, drizzling caramel topping on crullers for all eternity, or managing the inventory of a celestial donut shop, forced to account for every powdered sugar speck and jelly-filled imperfection. Even worse, what if he had to *make* the donuts, kneading and baking until his flabby fingers were permanently sticky and sore? Imagine Homer in a donut-judging competition, forced to critically evaluate each pastry, banishing all the flawed offerings to a fiery abyss of substandard dough. Or perhaps a hell where donuts were deemed unhealthy—where he had to eat quinoa and kale and other "healthy" replacements for donuts! Finally, what if Homer awoke each morning, only to realize that he had been transported into another world? He'd have to suffer the same hell every day but was only allowed to eat one donut for breakfast, with no more available afterwards. The horror!
